article.description: La NASA invita al mundo a conocer los detalles detrás de la historia del viaje de Europa Clipper, desde una visión lejana hasta una misión de exploración de espacio profundo de vanguardia, con el lanzamiento del nuevo documental de la agencia, “The Europa Concept.” El documental se transmitirá en NASA+, la aplicación de la NASA y el sitio web de la agencia a partir del lunes 23 de noviembre, y […]
article.explanation:
**Documental de NASA+ Captura el Viaje del Europa Clipper al Espacio Profundo**

La NASA ha lanzado un nuevo documental titulado “The Europa Concept”, que narra el proceso de desarrollo de la misión Europa Clipper, destinada a explorar la luna Europa de Júpiter. Este documental ofrece una mirada detrás de escena a los esfuerzos de ingenieros y científicos que han trabajado durante años para llevar esta misión a la realidad.

El Europa Clipper, que se lanzará en 2024, es el mayor spacecraft que la NASA ha enviado al espacio profundo. Su objetivo principal es investigar el océano que se cree existe bajo la superficie helada de Europa, en busca de condiciones que podrían permitir la vida. La misión se basa en décadas de investigación y en datos obtenidos por misiones anteriores, como las de Pioneer y Voyager.

El documental también destaca los desafíos enfrentados por el equipo, incluyendo la pandemia global y fenómenos climáticos extremos, que han puesto a prueba su dedicación y creatividad. A medida que se acerca el lanzamiento, la expectativa crece sobre los descubrimientos que Europa Clipper podría revelar sobre este intrigante mundo oceánico.
article.image_headline: La NASA lanza un documental sobre el viaje del Europa Clipper, explorando la posibilidad de vida en Europa.
article.original_title: NASA+ Documentary Captures Europa Clipper’s Journey Into Deep Space
article.source_body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) The NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept” takes audiences along on the journey to send a spacecraft to Jupiter’s moon Europa to determine whether the ocean beneath the moon’s icy shell has the ingredients for life. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech NASA invites the world behind the scenes to witness the story of Europa Clipper’s journey from a far-off vision to a cutting-edge deep space exploration mission with the release of the agency’s newest documentary, “The Europa Concept.” The documentary will air on NASA+ , the NASA app, and the agency’s website starting Monday, Nov. 23, and is coming soon to YouTube. It took decades of science, thousands of dedicated minds, endless creativity, and a whole lot of grit to get the Europa Clipper spacecraft to the launch pad in 2024. Now the orbiter, the largest NASA has ever sent into deep space, is two years into its five-year, 1.8 billion-mile (2.9 billion-kilometer) journey to the Jupiter system, where it will conduct flybys of Europa in search of the conditions for life in the vast ocean thought to hide beneath the moon’s icy surface. “The things we will learn from Europa Clipper will be so sensational, so fantastic, that everyone will be screaming for the next mission,” said Curt Niebur, program scientist in the Planetary Science Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “The only thing that matters is that we learn enough that we, in the broadest sense, want to do it again somewhere else — because that’s what exploration is.” Following a team of dedicated engineers and scientists on their yearslong efforts, the documentary captures how they developed a mission to Europa and built a spacecraft capable of surviving one of the most punishing radiation environments in our solar system. A product of Jupiter’s powerful magnetic field, that same radiation may have contributed to creating a potentially habitable environment on Europa. The moon, an object of fascination since its discovery by Galileo Galilei in 1610, only began to reveal its secrets with data obtained by NASA’s Pioneer 10 in 1973, followed the next year by Pioneer 11. But humanity didn’t get its first detailed look at Europa until Voyager 1’s flyby in 1979. More detailed glimpses of the moon followed from the agency’s Voyager 2, Galileo, Cassini, and Juno missions, each helping illuminate the way for Europa Clipper. Work officially began on the mission at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California in 2013, initiating an 11-year trek to build the spacecraft and its suite of nine science instruments in time to launch during a specific period of planetary alignment. Along the way, the team encountered plenty of unforeseen challenges, including a global pandemic and, just before launch on Oct. 14, 2024, a Category 5 hurricane and tornadoes near NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. “With Europa Clipper, we’ve taken the next step in solar system exploration, which will help us uncover the mysteries of an ocean world, and ultimately, whether potentially habitable worlds beyond our own exist,” said Jordan Evans, director of flight projects at JPL and the mission’s previous project manager. “This documentary pays tribute to the ingenuity, teamwork, and dedication that continue to make this incredible mission possible.” “The Europa Concept” takes audiences through the highs and lows alongside the thousands more who made Europa Clipper’s journey to the launch pad a success — and who will, in the coming years, be there to share the mission’s findings about humanity’s place in the cosmos. Find “The Europa Concept” on NASA+ here: https://plus.nasa.gov/video/the-europa-concept/ More about Europa Clipper Managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, JPL leads the development of the Europa Clipper mission in partnership with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, for NASA. The main spacecraft body was designed by APL in collaboration with JPL and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, and NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The Planetary Missions Program Office at NASA Marshall executes program management of the Europa Clipper mission. NASA’s Launch Services Program, based at Kennedy, managed the launch service for the Europa Clipper spacecraft. Find more information about Europa Clipper here: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/ -end- Media Contact Matthew Segal Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif. 818-354-8307 matthew.j.segal@jpl.nasa.gov Written by Kristy Hutchings 2026-086 Share Details Last Updated Nov 23, 2026 Related Terms Europa Clipper Europa

Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) será un pequeño sistema de energía de fisión que generará 20 kilovatios de electricidad, suficiente para alimentar aproximadamente 16 […]
article.explanation:
**NASA Busca Socios para Diseñar el Primer Reactor Nuclear para la Luna**

NASA está en la búsqueda de socios de la industria para desarrollar y probar el primer reactor nuclear destinado a generar electricidad en la Luna. Este proyecto, denominado Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1), tiene como objetivo proporcionar 20 kilovatios de energía, suficiente para abastecer aproximadamente 16 hogares estadounidenses durante un año. Esta energía será crucial para el establecimiento de una base lunar, apoyando infraestructuras como hábitats, sistemas de comunicación y equipos científicos.

Una de las ventajas del reactor nuclear es su capacidad para generar electricidad de manera continua, incluso durante las largas noches lunares, que pueden durar hasta dos semanas. Esto contrasta con la energía solar, que depende de la luz del sol. Según Brian Giblin, gerente del programa LR-1, contar con una fuente de energía confiable y segura es esencial para futuras exploraciones tanto en la Luna como en Marte.

Las propuestas para este proyecto deben presentarse antes del 21 de diciembre. Además, el reactor deberá cumplir con los estándares de seguridad del Departamento de Energía de EE. UU. Este avance en tecnología nuclear es parte de los esfuerzos de NASA para asegurar su liderazgo en la exploración espacial en las próximas décadas.

article.original_title: NASA Seeks Partners to Design First Nuclear Reactor for the Moon
article.source_body: Artist’s concept of a nuclear fission power system on the Moon’s surface. Credit: NASA NASA is seeking industry partners to develop and test the first nuclear reactor designed to provide electricity on the Moon, a major step toward establishing a sustained human presence on the lunar surface. Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) will be a small fission power system that will generate 20 kilowatts of electricity, enough to power approximately 16 average U.S. households annually on Earth. For NASA’s plans for a Moon Base , that energy could support future habitats, communications systems, rovers, scientific instruments, and other essential infrastructure. NASA aims to have a launch-ready system by 2030 and operate it on the Moon for at least five years after deployment. Unlike solar power, which depends on sunlight, a nuclear reactor can generate electricity continuously, including during the Moon’s approximately two-week-long nights. This capability will enable future lunar operations, particularly in locations where sunlight is limited or unavailable. “This request for proposals represents an important step forward as NASA partners with industry to establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface,” said Brian Giblin, NASA’s Lunar Reactor-1 program manager. “A reliable source of safe and abundant energy will be vital to future exploration of the lunar and Martian surface. Space nuclear systems will provide continuous power to NASA assets in any environment without dependency on sunlight.” NASA’s Space Power and Reactor Capabilities Request for Proposals incorporates feedback received after the agency released a draft proposal in August and hosted an industry day in September at the Ohio Aerospace Institute in Cleveland. The solicitation requires that the reactor must meet Department of Energy (DOE) safety standards for nuclear operations. While the primary purpose of the Request for Proposals is to advance the technology, testing, and flight design of LR-1, NASA may issue additional task orders to support the development of other space nuclear power systems. Proposals are due by Dec. 21. Nuclear power will be increasingly important to NASA’s space exploration ambitions. Lunar nights last about 14 Earth days, while dust storms on Mars can block sunlight for months. Farther from the Sun, solar power becomes progressively less effective. Nuclear systems offer a reliable source of electricity in these challenging environments. LR-1 is managed by the agency’s Space Reactors Division in partnership with the Department of Energy. The division is also responsible for the development of NASA’s Space Reactor‑1 (SR-1) Freedom. Scheduled to launch in 2028, SR-1 Freedom will deliver three SkyFall helicopters to Mars and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion, which uses electricity generated by a nuclear reactor to power spacecraft propulsion systems. This technology could enable future spacecraft to travel farther and undertake deep space missions that aren’t possible using conventional propulsion. Together, LR-1 and SR-1 Freedom are advancing nuclear power and propulsion technologies to enable a new era of space exploration. By investing in these technologies, NASA and DOE are helping secure America’s leadership in space for decades to come.

El NASA Space Apps Challenge, celebrado el 14 y 15 de noviembre, ha alcanzado un hito sin precedentes al registrar a 181,835 participantes en 593 eventos alrededor del mundo. article.description: La NASA seleccionó a tres empresas el miércoles para realizar trabajos de desarrollo de conceptos de capacidad de relé espacial en banda Ka que sean compatibles con las misiones actuales en el espacio, asegurando la continuidad del servicio para las naves espaciales existentes sin requerir modificaciones en sus sistemas a bordo. A través de este trabajo, la NASA buscará adquirir soluciones de extremo a extremo que incluyan espacio, tierra, lanzamiento, operaciones e integración […]
article.explanation:
**NASA Anuncia Premios de Relé Satelital Ka-Band para Comunicaciones Espaciales**

NASA ha seleccionado a tres empresas para desarrollar conceptos de capacidad de relé espacial en banda Ka, compatibles con misiones actuales. Este avance busca asegurar la continuidad del servicio para naves espaciales existentes sin necesidad de modificar sus sistemas a bordo.

Los contratos, bajo el programa Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3, son de precio fijo y permiten a NASA financiar el desarrollo desde la fase inicial hasta una demostración de vuelo en órbita. El periodo inicial de trabajo se extiende desde el 4 de noviembre de 2026 hasta el 3 de mayo de 2027, con opciones para continuar hasta 2029.

Las empresas seleccionadas son Astranis Space Technologies Corp., Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. y Viasat Inc., con valores máximos de contrato de $264.3 millones, $340.4 millones y $460.9 millones, respectivamente. Este esfuerzo es parte del programa SCaN de NASA, que busca reemplazar gradualmente la flota de satélites de seguimiento y datos, adoptando servicios comerciales para futuras misiones.

La implementación de servicios en banda Ka es crucial para misiones en órbita que no pueden modificar su hardware de vuelo, asegurando así la continuidad y sostenibilidad de las comunicaciones espaciales.

article.original_title: NASA Announces Ka-Band Satellite Relay Awards for Space Communications
article.source_body: Credit: NASA NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems. Through this work, NASA will aim to acquire end-to-end solutions that include space, ground, launch, operations, and integration elements, as one of many customers in the commercial marketplace. The awards, under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3 Broad Agency Announcement Appendix E, are firm-fixed-price contracts that give NASA the option to provide additional funding up to the award limit to advance from initial concept development and risk reduction to an in-orbit flight demonstration. The initial period of performance runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029. The contract awardees with maximum potential value inclusive of all future options are: Astranis Space Technologies Corp. for $264.3 million. Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. for $340.4 million. Viasat Inc. for $460.9 million. Facilitated through the agency’s SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) program’s Communications Services Project, this work supports NASA’s decision to gradually retire the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet and adopt commercial services for future missions. In addition to the commercial capabilities currently under development by the program’s industry partners, Ka-band services are needed to support select in-orbit missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware or transition to non-compatible commercial services. article.description: ¿Por qué algunos volcanes hacen erupción con espectaculares fuentes de lava mientras otros liberan lava de forma más
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Magma sobrecalentado podría alimentar altísimas fuentes de lava.**
**CATEGORÍA: volcanes**

Investigadores de la Universidad de Manchester, tras analizar material de la erupción del volcán Tajogaite en La Palma, descubrieron que el "sobrecalentamiento" del magma es clave para entender la violencia de las erupciones. Este proceso ocurre cuando la roca fundida alcanza temperaturas tan altas que disuelve las "semillas" microscópicas necesarias para formar cristales.

Los experimentos, que recrearon condiciones subterráneas, revelaron que este calor extremo puede retrasar la cristalización por más de ocho horas. Sin estos cristales, el magma mantiene una baja viscosidad, permaneciendo fluido por mucho más tiempo del esperado. Esto facilita un ascenso rápido hacia la superficie, lo que gatilla la formación de altísimas fuentes de lava impulsadas por gases.

En contraste, si el magma genera cristales temprano, se vuelve espeso y asciende lentamente, resultando en erupciones efusivas más calmas. Este hallazgo, publicado en *Nature Communications*, sugiere que la historia térmica del magma es fundamental para los modelos de pronóstico. Incorporar estos datos permitiría a los científicos prever con mayor precisión si un volcán presentará chorros de lava espectaculares o flujos de movimiento lento.

article.description: El ciclón tropical Xavier dio inicio a la temporada de tormentas de la cuenca con fuerza.
article.explanation:
**El tormentoso Pacífico Suroeste**

El Pacífico Suroeste ha sido escenario de intensas actividades ciclónicas, destacando el reciente ciclón tropical Xavier. Este fenómeno, que se formó el 15 de noviembre de 2026, se convirtió rápidamente en uno de los ciclones más potentes de noviembre en la región, alcanzando vientos máximos de hasta 220 kilómetros por hora. Su desarrollo se vio favorecido por temperaturas del mar de 29 grados Celsius y condiciones de baja cizalladura del viento.

Xavier, que se formó en un contexto de El Niño, es un ejemplo de cómo este fenómeno climático puede intensificar la actividad ciclónica. Investigaciones indican que durante años de El Niño, los ciclones tienden a fortalecerse más rápidamente y su actividad se desplaza hacia el noreste. Este ciclón, que causó daños en las Islas Cook, es considerado el más fuerte registrado en noviembre al este de la línea internacional de cambio de fecha.

A medida que Xavier se debilitó, se pronostica que la temporada ciclónica en el Pacífico Suroeste podría traer entre 11 y 15 tormentas nombradas, con un pico esperado en febrero. Esto resalta la creciente preocupación por el impacto de estos fenómenos en las comunidades costeras de la región.

article.original_title: The Stormy Southwest Pacific
article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory The Stormy Southwest Pacific Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search Even as the unusually quiet 2026 storm season winds down in the North Atlantic, seas have begun to stir on the other side of the world in the Southwest Pacific. On November 15, 2026 , the Fiji Meteorological Service began issuing updates about a slow-moving tropical disturbance northeast of Samoa and the Cook Islands. Within just a few days, it had become one of the most intense November tropical cyclones the region has seen in decades. Named Xavier , the system intensified rapidly , thriving in an environment with minimal wind shear and sea surface temperatures of 29 degrees Celsius (84 degrees Fahrenheit)—well above the threshold required to sustain and strengthen developing tropical cyclones . Xavier was the basin’s second named storm of the season, following only Wati , a short-lived storm that emerged in October. As Xavier developed, NASA satellite data showed the storm churning along the southwestern edge of a massive tongue of warm water spanning from the west coast of South America to the central Pacific—a telltale sign of the El Niño that has been present in the region since June . When the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this image at 02:53 Universal Time on November 17, 2026 (4:53 p.m. Cook Islands Time on November 16), forecasters estimated Xavier had maximum winds of about 195 kilometers (120 miles) per hour. Winds reached a peak intensity of 220 kilometers (140 miles) per hour later that day, a Category 5 storm on the cyclone intensity scale used in the region or a Category 4 on the Saffir-Simpson scale . The storm ranks as the strongest November tropical cyclone east of the international date line on record, noted Colorado State University hurricane expert Phil Klotzbach . Xavier’s formation east of the date line, near the northern Cook Islands, was unusual, but its easterly position aligns with research that indicates that storm activity in the region typically shifts northeast during El Niño years. Research also shows that El Niño tends to fuel storms that strengthen at an unusually rapid pace . According to news reports, Xavier damaged homes and caused power disruptions as it passed the northern Cook Islands. It then encountered dry air and a less favorable wind shear environment and slowly weakened as it pushed westward, reducing the threat that it posed to Samoa and American Samoa. Xavier is likely one of the first of several storms to affect the region in the coming months. A seasonal outlook from the Fiji Meteorological Service projects that the region could see between 11 and 15 named tropical cyclones this season, with the greatest risk east of the international date line. article.title: El tormentoso Pacífico Suroeste

6e494b32de360fdf8364.caption:
🌎 SISMONAUTA | CIENCIAS DEL OCÉANO

El ciclón tropical Xavier, el más fuerte de noviembre en el Pacífico Suroeste, causó daños en las Islas Cook.

El Pacífico Suroeste ha sido escenario de intensas actividades ciclónicas, destacando el reciente ciclón tropical Xavier. Este fenómeno, que se formó el 15 de noviembre de 2026, se convirtió rápidamente en uno de los ciclones más potentes de noviembre en la región, alcanzando vientos máximos de hasta 220 kilómetros por hora. Su desarrollo se vio favorecido por temperaturas del mar de 29 grados Celsius y condiciones de baja cizalladura del viento. Xavier, que se formó en un contexto de El Niño, es un ejemplo de cómo este fenómeno climático puede intensificar la actividad ciclónica. Investigaciones indican que durante años de El Niño, los ciclones tienden a fortalecerse más rápidamente y su actividad se desplaza hacia el noreste. Este ciclón, que causó daños en las Islas Cook, es considerado el más fuerte registrado en noviembre al este de la línea internacional de cambio de fecha. A medida que Xavier se debilitó, se pronostica que la temporada ciclónica en el Pacífico Suroeste podría traer entre 11 y 15 tormentas nombradas, con un pico esperado en febrero. Esto resalta la creciente preocupación por el impacto de estos fenómenos en las comunidades costeras de la región.

article.description: Los científicos han descubierto que la pegajosidad de la "nieve marina" submarina juega un papel sorprendentemente importante en la cantidad de carbono que llega al océano profundo. Las partículas más viscosas resisten la descomposición bacteriana y pueden transportar más de seis veces la cantidad de carbono a las profundidades, revelando una conexión inesperada entre el limo oceánico y el clima de la Tierra.
article.explanation:
**Superpoder climático oculto: Por qué parte de la "nieve" marina transporta seis veces más carbono**

Investigaciones recientes han revelado que la "nieve" marina, compuesta por partículas de desechos y organismos muertos, juega un papel crucial en el ciclo del carbono del océano. Este fenómeno, conocido como "marine snow", transporta grandes cantidades de carbono desde la superficie hacia el fondo marino. Se estima que más de 10 gigatoneladas de carbono son removidas anualmente de las aguas superficiales, pero solo alrededor de 2 gigatoneladas logran llegar a profundidades donde pueden permanecer almacenadas durante siglos.

Un estudio realizado por investigadores de la Universidad de California en San Diego y la Universidad de Lincoln ha identificado un factor clave en este proceso: la viscosidad de la nieve marina. Los hallazgos indican que las partículas más pegajosas pueden transportar más de seis veces la cantidad de carbono en comparación con aquellas de menor viscosidad. Esto se debe a que las partículas más densas resisten la degradación bacteriana durante más tiempo, permitiendo que desciendan a mayores profundidades.

Este descubrimiento no solo amplía nuestra comprensión del ciclo del carbono, sino que también tiene implicaciones en otros ecosistemas donde las interacciones entre bacterias y mucosidades son fundamentales, como en los arrecifes de coral y la salud digestiva humana. La investigación destaca la complejidad de lo que antes se consideraba un material simple, revelando un paisaje interno que influye en el comportamiento bacteriano y, por ende, en los procesos biológicos del planeta.

article.description: Una tormenta de nieve generalizada y temprana cubrió de blanco las montañas de California a mediados de noviembre de 2026.
article.explanation:
**Agarra vuelo la temporada de nieve en la Sierra**

La temporada de nieve en la Sierra Nevada de California comenzó con fuerza, gracias a un sistema de tormentas que trajo precipitaciones significativas. El 13 de noviembre de 2026, se registraron acumulaciones de nieve de aproximadamente 30 centímetros en áreas montañosas, como Donner Pass, lo que generó complicaciones en el tráfico, incluyendo el cierre de la autopista Interestatal 80.

Este evento marcó el inicio de una serie de tormentas que se pronostica continuarán afectando la región. La Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica (NOAA) emitió una advertencia de tormenta invernal para las áreas de mayor altitud, anticipando condiciones de viaje difíciles y acumulaciones de nieve que podrían alcanzar hasta 120 centímetros en elevaciones superiores a 2,400 metros.

Los centros de esquí, como Mammoth Mountain, también reportaron entre 23 y 33 centímetros de nueva nieve, lo que podría beneficiar la temporada de esquí. Sin embargo, las autoridades advierten sobre la posibilidad de condiciones climáticas severas, lo que podría afectar tanto a residentes como a visitantes en la región. La llegada de más tormentas en los próximos días sugiere que la temporada de nieve apenas comienza.

article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Sierra Snow Season Spins Up Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search November 12 November 14 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison November 12 November 14 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison November 12 November 14 Curtain Toggle 2-Up California’s Sierra Nevada got an early taste of wintry weather when one of the first major snowfalls of the water year arrived on November 13, 2026. A moisture-laden storm delivered heavy rains to lower elevations in the Sacramento area and snow accumulations of around a foot to some mountainous areas. The recent bout of wet weather was the first in a quick succession of Pacific storms bringing rain, snow, and wind to the U.S. West in mid-November. The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured this image (right) of fresh snow in the Sierra Nevada on the morning of November 14, during a lull between weather systems. Two days earlier (left), the mountains were mostly bare, with snow appearing only at the highest elevations. Nearly 12 inches (30 centimeters) of snow fell at Donner Pass, northwest of Lake Tahoe, on November 13, according to the Central Sierra Snow Laboratory . The accumulation snarled traffic on Interstate 80 in the area, prompting officials to close the highway in both directions that evening. To the south, the ski resort at Mammoth Mountain reported 9 to 13 inches (23 to 33 centimeters) of new snow, and officials at Yosemite National Park closed several roads ahead of the storm. More wet weather and mountain snow are forecast to follow . The National Weather Service (NWS) issued a winter storm warning for portions of the Sierras above 5,000 feet (1,500 meters) in elevation from November 18 to 20. NWS warned of difficult-to-impossible travel conditions, gusty winds, and snow accumulations of around 4 feet (120 centimeters) possible above 8,000 feet (2,400 meters). Utilizados para propulsar satélites y profundos […]
article.explanation:
**NASA Anuncia el Desafío de Cohetes Eléctricos de Media Potencia para Empresas de EE. UU.**

NASA ha lanzado una nueva competencia destinada a empresas estadounidenses para desarrollar prototipos de propulsores eléctricos de media potencia, específicamente los thrusters de efecto Hall. Esta tecnología es fundamental para futuras operaciones y exploraciones espaciales, ya que permite un uso más eficiente del propulsor, utilizando diez veces menos que los cohetes químicos equivalentes.

El desafío, denominado AMPERE, ofrece un total de $500,000, que se dividirán entre dos empresas ganadoras. El objetivo es acelerar el desarrollo de sistemas de propulsión que serán esenciales para misiones futuras de NASA y del sector comercial. La competencia se llevará a cabo en tres fases, comenzando con la presentación de diseños conceptuales y planes de fabricación.

Los equipos seleccionados en la primera fase tendrán la oportunidad de avanzar a la segunda, donde desarrollarán prototipos en colaboración con personal de NASA. Además, podrán acceder a tecnologías de propulsores desarrolladas por la agencia, utilizando criptón como propulsor. La fase final incluirá pruebas de los prototipos en las instalaciones de NASA sin costo para los participantes. 

El desafío está abierto para inscripciones hasta el 27 de enero de 2027, lo que representa una oportunidad significativa para las empresas involucradas en la innovación espacial.

article.original_title: NASA Announces Mid-Power Electric Rocket Challenge for US Companies
article.source_body: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) The Hall thruster is part of an Solar Electric Propulsion (SEP) system that uses 10 times less propellant than equivalent chemical rockets. Image Credit: NASA/Michelle M. Murphy (Wyle Information Systems, LLC) NASA launched a new competition inviting U.S. companies to produce prototypes of mid-power Hall effect thrusters – a type of electric propulsion system considered crucial for future space operations and exploration. Hall effect thrusters use an electric field to accelerate a propellant gas, producing efficient thrust for long-duration missions. Used for propelling satellites and deep space robotic vehicles, Hall effect thruster systems are critical technology. NASA’s Advanced Mid-Power Electric Rocket (AMPERE) Challenge is offering $500,000, split between two winning U.S. companies, to accelerate the maturation of mid-power systems that could be foundational to supporting future NASA and commercial missions. Interested parties can learn more at an AMPERE Virtual Industry Day hosted by NASA on Thursday, Nov. 19. “This challenge approach seeks to remove key barriers and facilitate commercialization by providing access to NASA subject matter expertise, state-of-the-art technologies, and world-class facilities at no cost to challenge winners,” said Dr. Jason Frieman, AMPERE project co-owner at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland. “We hope participants will see this as an opportunity to demonstrate their capabilities to NASA and other government and commercial stakeholders.” The competition is the first of NASA’s Tech Maturation Prize series, which seeks to accelerate development of breakthrough technologies in support of NASA missions while strengthening the U.S. space economy. The competition includes three phases. In Phase 1, each participating team will submit a concept design, manufacturing plan, and cost and performance projections. NASA may select two winners to advance to Phase 2, where teams will develop prototypes and collaborate with NASA personnel. Through no-cost licensing, these teams can gain early access to NASA-developed Hall effect thruster technologies that use krypton as a propellant. In Phase 3, prototypes will be tested at NASA Glenn at no cost to the participating teams. In total, two winning teams may be selected to receive up to $250,000 each. The AMPERE Challenge is open for registration until Jan. 27, 2027, at 5 p.m. EST. The challenge supports the Advanced Mid-Power Electric Rocket project, managed by NASA Glenn and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The project is funded by the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate . Yet2 administers the challenge through a contract with the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate. article.description: A mountain range can bear the marks of events from tens of millions of years ago. The challenge lies in determining when each mark was created. In southern Türkiye's Central Taurides, scientists have developed a method to date some of these ancient movements by examining tiny calcite deposits that formed as faults shifted. This new timeline alters the region's geological history. Researchers discovered a previously unrecognized period during which parts of the crust slid laterally, between the Early Eocene and Early Miocene. They also found that the region's later extension began around 25 million years ago, earlier than previously believed.
article.explanation: Una cordillera puede llevar las marcas de eventos de hace decenas de millones de años. El desafío radica en determinar cuándo se creó cada marca. En los Taurides Centrales del sur de Türkiye, los científicos han desarrollado un método para datar algunos de estos antiguos movimientos al examinar pequeños depósitos de calcita que se formaron a medida que las fallas se desplazaban. Esta nueva cronología altera la historia geológica de la región. Los investigadores descubrieron un período previamente no reconocido durante el cual partes de la corteza se deslizaron lateralmente, entre el Eoceno Temprano y el Mioceno Temprano. También encontraron que la posterior extensión de la región comenzó hace alrededor de 25 millones de años, antes de lo que se creía anteriormente.

article.description: Las precipitaciones de invierno ayudaron a despertar semillas latentes en el norte de Chile, alfombrando el desierto con la que podría ser la floración más extensa de la región de la era satelital.
article.explanation:
**Las lluvias de El Niño pintan el Atacama**

El fenómeno de El Niño ha traído consigo un cambio notable en el desierto de Atacama, uno de los lugares más áridos del planeta. En la primavera austral de 2026, tras un invierno inusualmente húmedo, el desierto se transformó en un espectáculo de colores, con extensas áreas cubiertas de flores. Este evento ha sido catalogado como el más significativo en términos de extensión, intensidad y duración desde que se utilizan imágenes satelitales para su estudio.

Las lluvias, que comenzaron en julio, fueron alimentadas por un río atmosférico y resultaron en uno de los episodios de lluvia más intensos en décadas. Esto permitió que semillas que habían permanecido inactivas en el suelo germinaran, dando lugar a un desierto florido que ha capturado la atención de científicos y turistas por igual. Investigadores de la Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso han estado utilizando datos satelitales y drones para mapear la biodiversidad de estas floraciones, lo que podría ser crucial para la planificación del uso del suelo y la conservación en la región.

article.original_title: El Niño Rains Paint the Atacama
article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory El Niño Rains Paint the Atacama Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search September 14 October 24 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 14 October 24 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 14 October 24 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Parts of the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, normally one of the driest places on Earth, turned red-purple, green, and white in austral spring 2026 following an unusually wet winter. The rain woke seeds lying dormant in the soil, setting off what scientists say may be the most extensive desierto florido , or “flowering desert,” of the satellite era. The rains came as El Niño was strengthening in the tropical Pacific. During an El Niño, the subtropical Pacific high that normally keeps the region dry weakens, while a blocking high tends to form in the South Pacific near the tip of South America. Together, these shifts push the Southern Hemisphere storm track equatorward. Beginning in mid-July, a series of storm fronts fed by an atmospheric river brought one of the heaviest July rain events in decades to a long stretch of Chile, from the Atacama region south to Los Lagos, according to Chile’s national weather service (Dirección Meteorológica de Chile). In August, back-to-back winter storms blanketed parts of the Atacama Desert in rare snow . The spring blooms that followed are visible in these satellite image pairs, which show the desert at different stages of flowering on September 14 (left) and on October 24 (right). The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 acquired the September images, and the OLI on Landsat 9 acquired the October images. The pair above shows a part of the desert about 30 kilometers (20 miles) southwest of Copiapó, near the eastern sector of Desierto Florido National Park. The red-purple areas prominent in the October 24 scene are vast blooms of pata de guanaco, most likely Cistanthe longiscapa or another Cistanthe species, according to Roberto Chávez, a remote sensing scientist at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso. Patches of red-purple Cistanthe are visible during a bloom in the Atacama Desert, shown in this photograph taken on October 24, 2026. Matías Pérez-Evens and Roberto O. Chávez/LabGRS-Instituto de Geografía- Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso. Chávez and colleagues photographed the Cistanthe blooms (above) in the area that same day. They were in the field to study the bloom with satellite data, drones, and digital cameras. The project aims to use these data to map how the bloom’s biodiversity changes across space and over time, to inform land-use planners and conservation managers. The pair below shows another part of the blooming desert, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) southwest of Copiapó. It lies within a priority area of the desert cited for its biological significance, including the flowering landscape. september 14 october 24 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison september 14 october 24 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison september 14 october 24 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Cistanthe is abundant here in the October view, but the September scene (left) reveals another desert beauty. The green areas capped with white are blooms of suspiros, or Nolana , probably Nolana baccata , according to Andres Moreira-Muñoz, a scientist at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso who studies plant geography. The researchers photographed the Nolana -covered hillsides below on September 24, 2026. White Nolana blankets a hillside in the Atacama Desert during a bloom, shown in this photograph taken on September 24, 2026. Matías Pérez-Evens and Roberto O. Chávez/LabGRS-Instituto de Geografía- Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso. Satellite data have been key to understanding the Atacama’s blooms. A 2014 study used Landsat observations to map where flowering and fog-fed plants grow around the Copiapó dune field. And a 2019 study used NASA’s long-term vegetation record to identify 13 Atacama Desert blooms between 1981 and 2015. Compared with those past blooms, the 2026 event stands out. “This instance of the ‘blooming desert’ phenomenon appears to be the most significant to date—in terms of its extent, intensity, and duration,” Moreira-Muñoz said, “at least since we began using remote sensing.” NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Photos by Matías Pérez-Evens and Roberto O. Chávez/LabGRS-Instituto de Geografía- Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso, Chile, acquired during Fondecyt Regular Project 1251184 (ANID, Chile): Spatiotemporal variation of Flowering Desert biodiversity via multispectral remote sensing. article.explanation:
**NASA cubrirá la partida de la 35.ª misión de reabastecimiento de SpaceX desde la Estación Espacial**

NASA y SpaceX están en la fase final de la 35.ª misión de reabastecimiento, con un lanzamiento programado para el 18 de noviembre. El vehículo Dragon, que transporta más de 6,300 libras de suministros y experimentos científicos, se separará de la Estación Espacial Internacional (EEI) y comenzará su regreso a la Tierra.

Entre los experimentos que regresan se encuentran un constructo de vaso sanguíneo impreso en 3D, utilizado para estudiar el envejecimiento vascular y enfermedades cardiovasculares. También se enviarán organoides tumorales tratados en la EEI, que ayudarán a los investigadores a encontrar nuevas formas de mejorar los tratamientos contra el cáncer. Además, se analizarán muestras microbianas para comprender mejor la resistencia a los antibióticos en el espacio.

El regreso del Dragon está sujeto a las condiciones meteorológicas, y se espera que el aterrizaje se realice frente a la costa de California. Aunque NASA no transmitirá el aterrizaje, proporcionará actualizaciones a través de su blog. Esta misión es parte de un esfuerzo continuo para avanzar en la investigación científica y preparar futuras misiones a la Luna y Marte.

article.original_title: NASA to Cover 35th SpaceX Resupply Mission Space Station Departure
article.source_body: A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft supporting the company’s 34th commercial resupply services mission for NASA departs the International Space Station following its undocking from the Harmony module’s forward port. Credit: NASA/Jessica Meir NASA and its international partners are set to receive scientific research samples and hardware as a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft departs the International Space Station no earlier than Wednesday, Nov. 18, for its return to Earth. Pending weather conditions, the Dragon spacecraft will undock from the Harmony module’s space-facing port at 11:05 a.m. EST, following a command sent by ground controllers at SpaceX’s facility in Hawthorne, California. NASA’s live coverage of undocking and departure begins at 10:45 a.m., streaming through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live NASA and SpaceX are monitoring weather forecasts and targeting splashdown off the California coast no earlier than 1:50 a.m. Thursday, Nov. 19 (10:50 p.m. PST Nov. 18). Teams will adjust plans as needed based on splashdown conditions in the Dragon recovery area and will provide updates on splashdown timing when available. NASA will not stream the splashdown but will post updates on its space station blog . Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth. The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth. Frozen tumor organoids treated aboard the station also will return, helping researchers identify new ways to improve cancer treatments and advance personalized medicine. Scientists will analyze frozen microbial samples to better understand how antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive, adapt, and evolve in space. In addition, a lighting system will return after more than three years aboard the space station, where researchers tested its potential to support astronauts’ sleep and well-being during long-duration missions. Filled with more than 6,300 pounds of crew supplies, science investigations, and equipment, the spacecraft arrived at the space station on Oct. 15. It launched two days earlier on a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida for the agency’s SpaceX 35th commercial resupply services mission. For more than 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs not possible on Earth. The space station helps NASA understand and overcome the challenges of human spaceflight, expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit, and build on the foundation for long-duration missions to the Moon, as part of the Artemis and Moon Base programs, and to Mars. Get breaking news, images, and features from the space station on Instagram , Facebook , and X . article.description: Los datos abiertos de la misión Fermi de la NASA ayudaron a un equipo internacional de científicos a desarrollar un método para encontrar púlsares cerca de un millón de veces más rápido que antes.
article.explanation:
**Datos científicos de la NASA impulsan nuevo método para descubrir púlsares difíciles de encontrar**

Un equipo internacional de científicos ha desarrollado un método innovador que permite identificar púlsares en los datos de la NASA hasta un millón de veces más rápido que los enfoques anteriores. Este avance se basa en 15 años de datos del Telescopio Espacial Fermi, que observa el cielo cada tres horas.

Los púlsares son núcleos de estrellas muertas que giran rápidamente y emiten radiación, similar a un faro. Sin embargo, encontrarlos en los datos de Fermi es complicado, ya que la señal de un púlsar se mezcla con el ruido de otras fuentes gamma. El nuevo método, inspirado en técnicas de criptografía, transforma la búsqueda en un problema geométrico, facilitando la identificación de estos objetos celestes.

El equipo logró detectar el púlsar PSR J1622−7204, que gira 261 veces por segundo, utilizando solo 10 horas de tiempo de procesamiento en una computadora estándar. Este descubrimiento resalta la importancia de la política de datos abiertos de la NASA, que permite a los investigadores acceder a información valiosa y aplicar enfoques novedosos en sus análisis.

article.original_title: NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars
article.source_body: 5 min read NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, illustrated here, scans the entire sky every three hours as it orbits Earth. Its publicly available data helps scientists find the rapidly spinning cores of dead stars, known as pulsars. NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/Chris Smith (USRA/GESTAR) An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. A paper describing the results published Thursday in the Physical Review Letters. Using 15 years of data from NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor. By comparison, the previous best method failed to find the pulsar, despite using enough computing power that a standard processor would take 600 years to perform the calculation. A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, much like a lighthouse. Finding pulsars in gamma-ray data is extraordinarily difficult because Fermi detects only a tiny number of photons from a given pulsar, mixed in with background noise from other gamma-ray-emitting sources and the broader universe. To find the signal, researchers must accurately guess several unknowns at once: how fast the star spins, how quickly the spin is slowing down, and precisely where it sits in the sky. Searching every possible combination would require an impossible number of computations. “We don’t see every rotation from the pulsar, and we can’t just count the rotations to work out where the photon came from,” said lead author Daniel Pook-Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute) in Germany. “We have a four-dimensional grid, and we must search each direction with millions of trials in it. There’s just not enough computing power on Earth to do it.” This artist’s concept shows a pulsar, which emits light in regular pulses as it rotates, like a cosmic lighthouse. Pulsars are dense remnants of exploded stars, and are part of a class of objects called neutron stars. Openly available data from NASA’s Fermi space telescope can help scientists spot pulsars in the gamma-ray spectrum. NASA/JPL-Caltech Traditionally, scientists have searched for these pulsars by breaking Fermi data into smaller chunks and analyzing them by crowdsourcing computing power from volunteers around the world. Even with these volunteers contributing their computers’ unused processing power to run searches, it typically took the equivalent of hundreds of computer-years to identify a single pulsar. Gazith and Zackay realized that the search could be transformed into a geometry problem: finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, or a regularly spaced array of points. This lattice technique draws on algorithms developed by cryptographers trying to break encryption systems designed to resist code-breaking by future quantum computers . The method has also been used to help make satellite navigation systems more efficient. “We have nothing to do with cryptography in our analysis here, but those algorithms can help us solve the problem of searching for pulsars in our data,” Gazith said. Each trial run of the algorithm took about five minutes on a single computer core — easily doable on a standard laptop, which usually has between two and eight cores. Once the lattice method identified a pulsar candidate, the researchers confirmed it by feeding in the full Fermi data set, revealing a signal so strong it could not be a chance occurrence. The team’s next goal is even more ambitious: finding pulsars in binary systems, where a pulsar orbits a star. These discoveries have long been considered out of reach because a companion star’s gravity distorts the signal in ways that have made these pulsars essentially impossible to discover with traditional methods. “We know that there are probably tens or maybe even hundreds of these pulsars in the data set that we just couldn’t find,” said Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute who co-authored the study. “The next goal is to extend the searches and use the combination of the new algorithm and the crowdsourced computing power from volunteers in our Einstein@Home program to hopefully find many new pulsars that we think should be there.” This view of the gamma-ray sky is constructed from one year of Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) observations. The map shows the rate at which the LAT instrument detects gamma rays with energies above 300 million electron volts — about 120 million times the energy of visible light — from different sky directions. Brighter colors equal higher rates. Fermi’s openly available data archive contains a wealth of information that has supercharged scientific studies about the extreme universe. NASA/DOE/Fermi LAT Collaboration The discovery would not have happened without NASA’s longstanding, Gold Standard Science policy of making its science data, including data from Fermi, freely available to anyone. Launched in 2008, Fermi surveys the entire sky every three hours, observing the universe in gamma rays — the highest-energy form of light. After an initial one-year calibration period, all Fermi data became fully public and continues to be released as soon as it is processed. “The nice thing about NASA data is it’s all open,” Clark said. “All 18 years of Fermi data have been made public, and the data just keeps growing.” That openness allowed researchers from outside the Fermi mission, including the cryptography-inspired team, to apply a completely new approach to the dataset. NASA’s support for the science community, through open software and tools such as NASA’s Fermitools , enabled the team to prepare their dataset before beginning their analysis. The Fermi mission has grown its catalog from a few hundred gamma ray sources to thousands, with new findings emerging as scientists apply fresh ideas to the same data. “Any search that one team is doing, another team can just go and do that and check the search,” said Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “It’s made all of the science better.” For more information about NASA’s Fermi mission, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/fermi By Amanda Moon Adams Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer Share Details Last Updated Nov 19, 2026 Related Terms Open Science Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope Goddard Space Flight Center Pulsars Explore More 7 min read NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger Article 1 day ago 2 min read NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records Article 2 days ago 5 min read NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of… Article 1 week ago Keep Exploring Discover Related Topics Missions Humans in Space Climate Change Solar System

article.explanation: Un encuentro raro a casi 2,000 pies bajo la superficie del océano le dio a los científicos una oportunidad extraordinaria para filmar a una de las criaturas más inusuales del fondo marino. Investigadores del Instituto de Investigación del Acuario de la Bahía de Monterey (MBARI) avistaron un pez barreleye (Macropinna microstoma), una especie misteriosa conocida por su cabeza transparente y ojos notables que pueden rotar para seguir a su presa. El descubrimiento ocurrió durante una expedición a bordo del buque de investigación David Packard. Fue solo la undécima vez que los científicos de MBARI han encontrado este pez esquivo durante casi cuatro décadas de exploración oceánica. Miembros del Equipo de Biodiversidad y Bioóptica de MBARI estaban investigando la vida marina aproximadamente a 90 kilómetros (55 millas) de la costa cuando avistaron el pez a unos 600 metros (1,970 pies) debajo de la superficie. Usando el vehículo operado remotamente (ROV) Doc Ricketts, los investigadores estaban filmando y recolectando organismos de aguas profundas cuando apareció el visitante inesperado. "Ver un pez barreleye es un regalo raro. La tripulación de todo el barco se unió al equipo científico en la sala de control, hipnotizados por este animal notable.

El descubrimiento ocurrió durante una expedición a bordo del buque de investigación David Packard. Fue solo la undécima vez que los científicos de MBARI han encontrado este pez esquivo durante casi cuatro décadas de exploración oceánica. Miembros del Equipo de Biodiversidad y Bioóptica de MBARI estaban investigando la vida marina aproximadamente a 90 kilómetros (55 millas) de la costa cuando avistaron el pez a unos 600 metros (1,970 pies) debajo de la superficie. Usando el vehículo operado remotamente (ROV) Doc Ricketts, los investigadores estaban filmando y recolectando organismos de aguas profundas cuando apareció el visitante inesperado. "Ver un pez barreleye es un regalo raro. La tripulación de todo el barco se unió al equipo científico en la sala de control, hipnotizados por este animal notable.

article.explanation:
**El giroavión Dragonfly de la NASA con destino a Titán recibe sus ojos**

Los instrumentos científicos del giroavión Dragonfly de la NASA están comenzando a llegar al Laboratorio de Física Aplicada de Johns Hopkins en Maryland. Este rotorcraft, del tamaño de un automóvil, tiene como misión explorar Titán, la luna más grande de Saturno. Recientemente, se instaló DragonCam, un conjunto de siete cámaras diseñadas para caracterizar la superficie de Titán tanto durante el vuelo como en el suelo.

Cada cámara está protegida en un recinto aislante que la resguarda de las extremas temperaturas de Titán, que alcanzan los -290 grados Fahrenheit. Además, un sistema de iluminación LED permitirá a los científicos observar la composición de los materiales en la superficie, incluso durante la larga noche de Titán, que dura casi ocho días terrestres.

La capacidad de DragonCam para capturar imágenes desde diferentes ángulos proporcionará vistas detalladas y panorámicas del paisaje titánico. Esto es crucial para entender los procesos geológicos de esta luna. La misión está programada para lanzarse en julio de 2028 y se espera que llegue a Titán a finales de 2034.

article.original_title: NASA’s Titan-Bound Dragonfly Rotorcraft Gets Its Eyes
article.source_body: Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. From left, technicians Chad Cook and Seth Harvey install the high-resolution microscopic imager – part of the seven-camera DragonCam science imaging suite – onto NASA’s Dragonfly rotorcraft at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, on Nov. 6, 2026. NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/Ed Whitman First to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize Titan ’s surface at multiple scales during flight and while on the ground. By mid-November, all seven cameras developed and built by Malin Space Science Systems had been installed in their insulated housings, tested, and integrated into the rotorcraft. Each camera will look out at Titan through a window in a foam enclosure that insulates the cameras and Dragonfly’s interior from Titan’s cryogenic environment, where ambient temperatures reach minus 290 degrees Fahrenheit. A configurable LED array, built at APL and spanning the light spectrum from the infrared to the ultraviolet, provides information about the color of surface materials at the sampling site and helps scientists make inferences about their composition. During Titan’s long night, which spans nearly eight Earth days, these observations also may allow DragonCam to identify organic molecules that fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The LED illumination also allows us to see Titan as human eyes would. “One of the most exciting things about Dragonfly is that we’ll be able to see Titan from perspectives we’ve never had before,” said Elizabeth Turtle, Dragonfly principal investigator at APL. “With the capability to take images when Dragonfly is on the surface as well as while flying, DragonCam will give us both detailed views and sweeping panoramas of Titan’s landscape, as well as insight into the processes that shaped this extraordinary world. Seeing these cameras become part of the Dragonfly lander is an exciting milestone that brings us another step closer to this unprecedented exploration.” Matthew Clark (left) and Michael Ravine of Malin Space Science Systems check DragonCam’s seven science cameras and digital video recorder before shipping them to Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) for integration and testing onto NASA’s Dragonfly rotorcraft. MSSS/Olawale Oluwo In addition to these science cameras, Dragonfly has two navigation cameras, also built by Malin Space Science Systems, that were installed this summer. “We are extremely pleased to have delivered the DragonCam cameras,” said Michael Ravine, DragonCam development manager and a Dragonfly co-investigator from Malin Space Science Systems. “Now to have them on the Dragonfly spacecraft, taking images, it’s so much easier to picture how they will work on Titan. These will be our eyes to see and explore this whole new world.” Two forward-mounted cameras — a wide-angle camera (WAC) and medium-angle camera (MAC) — are designed to capture images of the terrain in front of Dragonfly. The forward WAC offers a 90-degree field of view, while the forward MAC overlaps with the WAC, capturing part of that field of view at a higher resolution. Combined, the images from these two cameras provide a stereoscopic perspective from the front of the lander. Together with two additional side-mounted WACs, the system is able to capture panoramic views of the Titan landscape. Panoramic view of the cleanroom at APL, Johns Hopkins APL, consisting of three images taken by Dragonfly’s forward- and side-facing wide-angle cameras (WACs). At left is Dragonfly’s top deck, including its circular high-gain antenna (seen edge-on), and members of the APL and Malin Space Science Systems integration and testing team are visible in the control room windows. The images – taken on Nov. 9, 2026, shortly after the DragonCam camera suite was installed on the lander – have a yellow tint because DragonCam captures light differently than the human eye sees it. NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/MSSS Two downward-facing WACs provide views of the surface beneath Dragonfly, helping the mission team decide if a landing spot is safe for deploying Dragonfly’s sample-collecting tool, known as DrACO, or Drill for Acquisition of Complex Organics, and its seismometer. A high-resolution microscopic imager will aim at DrACO’s drill site to pick out the details in millimeter-sized sand grains around the sampling location. “DragonCam will give us critical context for the samples collected by DrACO,” said Carolyn Ernst, the DragonCam instrument scientist at APL. “We’ll be collecting materials at multiple sites across Titan, and the images from the cameras will help us relate the samples to Titan’s broader landscape and piece together the story of its geology.” DragonCam is a suite of cameras aboard NASA’s Dragonfly rotorcraft designed to capture images of Titan’s surface from the ground and during flight. DragonCam will help scientists study landforms and surface processes at multiple scales, providing new insights into Titan’s geology and environment. This animation highlights the elements of DragonCam and how its imaging capabilities will support Dragonfly’s scientific investigations NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/Zac Swanson Components of Dragonfly’s other instrument packages , DraGNS (Gamma-ray and Neutron Spectrometer), DraGMet (Geophysics and Meteorology), DraMS (Mass Spectrometer) and DrACO, are set for delivery, integration and testing over the next several months. Dragonfly is scheduled to launch in July 2028 and reach Titan in late 2034. For more on NASA’s Dragonfly mission, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/dragonfly Karen Fox / Molly Wasser Headquarters, Washington 240-285-5155 / 240-419-1732 karen.c.fox@nasa.gov / molly.l.wasser@nasa.gov Mike Buckley Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory 443-567-3145 michael.buckley@jhuapl.edu

article.original_title: NASA Sets Coverage for Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Launch, Prelaunch
article.source_body: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 24 mission launched Saturday, April 11, 2026, aboard the company’s Cygnus XL spacecraft atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will deliver approximately 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. Credit: Northrop Grumman NASA, Northrop Grumman, and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 10:47 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, for the next launch delivering science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. The agency also will hold a prelaunch media teleconference on Monday, Nov. 23. Filled with approximately 11,000 pounds of cargo, the Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, will launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25. After arriving at the International Space Station, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, who are living and working aboard the space station, will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture the Cygnus XL on Tuesday, Dec. 1. Ground controllers then will install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. NASA’s live launch and docking coverage will stream through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live Highlights of space station research and technology demonstrations being delivered aboard this Cygnus XL spacecraft include experiments to improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, predict cancer spread, and advance treatments for muscle loss, as well as improve radiation sensing and advance food production for future long-duration missions. The spacecraft is scheduled to remain at the orbiting laboratory until May 2027, then depart with several thousand pounds of disposal items and other unneeded cargo, burning up harmlessly during re-entry. Northrop Grumman named the spacecraft the S.S. James “Jim” A. Lovell in honor of the former NASA astronaut. Lovell flew four missions, including Gemini VII, Gemini XII, Apollo 8, and the Apollo 13 mission around the Moon. Monday, Nov. 23 12 p.m.: Prelaunch teleconference will stream on NASA’s YouTube channel with the following participants: Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager, NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program Jennifer Buchli, chief scientist, NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program Dave Schiller, vice president, civil space and sciences, Northrop Grumman Jared Metter, director, flight reliability, SpaceX To participate in the teleconference, media must contact the NASA Johnson Space Center newsroom for call details by 11 a.m., Nov. 23, at: jsccommu@mail.nasa.gov or 281-483-5111. To ask questions, media must dial in no later than 10 minutes before the start of the call. The agency’s media credentialing policy is available online. Additional prelaunch updates will be available on NASA’s space station blog . Sunday, Nov. 29 10:25 a.m.: Launch coverage begins 10:47 a.m.: Launch Tuesday, Dec. 1 1:10 a.m.: Arrival coverage begins 2:35 a.m.: Capture NASA website launch coverage Launch day coverage of the mission will be available on the NASA website . Coverage will include live streaming and blog updates beginning no earlier than 10 a.m. on Nov. 29, as the countdown milestones occur. On-demand streaming video on NASA+ and photos of the launch will be available shortly after liftoff. For questions about countdown coverage, contact the NASA Kennedy Space Center newsroom at 321-867-2468. Follow countdown coverage on our International Space Station blog for updates. Attend launch virtually Members of the public can register to attend this launch virtually. NASA’s virtual guest program for this mission also includes curated launch resources, notifications about related opportunities or changes, and a stamp for the NASA virtual guest passport following launch. article.explanation:
**NASA lanza concurso para estudiantes sobre sistemas de energía nuclear**

NASA ha inaugurado el "Power to Explore Student Challenge", un concurso dirigido a estudiantes desde jardín infantil hasta 12° básico en Estados Unidos. Este desafío busca fomentar el aprendizaje sobre sistemas de energía nuclear en el espacio, invitando a los participantes a imaginar cómo estas "baterías" nucleares podrían impulsar la exploración lunar.

Los estudiantes deberán presentar un ensayo de 200 palabras y una ilustración original que refleje su visión de una base lunar alimentada por energía nuclear. Además, se les pide que describan un "superpoder" personal que contribuiría a la misión. Las inscripciones están abiertas hasta el 1 de marzo de 2027.

El concurso tiene como objetivo preparar a la próxima generación de exploradores para enfrentar los desafíos de la exploración lunar, especialmente en regiones con condiciones extremas. Según Carl Sandifer, gerente de programas de la División de Reactores Espaciales de NASA, la energía nuclear podría ser clave para operar en áreas permanentemente sombreadas y mantener instrumentos en funcionamiento durante las largas noches lunares.

Los ganadores de cada categoría de grado recibirán un viaje al Centro de Investigación Glenn de NASA en Cleveland, donde aprenderán sobre las tecnologías que hacen posibles las misiones espaciales.

article.original_title: NASA Launches Nuclear Power Systems Student Contest
article.source_body: The thematics for the 2026-2027 Radioisotope Power Systems Power to Explore Student Challenge Credit: NASA / David Lam NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027. Every mission requires a power source. Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions. Nuclear power could sustain human life and allow researchers to study the resource-rich environment despite freezing temperatures, long nights, and deep craters that never see sunlight. “As NASA returns to the Moon and establishes a lunar base where astronauts will live, work, and explore, we need to build an infrastructure to make it all possible. Nuclear power could enable exploration in the permanently shadowed regions near the Moon’s South Pole, carry robust science payloads over long distances, and keep instruments warm through the lunar night,” said Carl Sandifer, a program manager for NASA’s Space Reactors Division at the agency’s headquarters in Washington. “NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design. We cannot wait to see what they come up with!” Entries include a 200-word essay and an original illustration. Essays should describe one of the students’ unique powers that will help the mission. Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using both radioisotope and fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable. Judges will review entries in three grade-level categories: K-4, 5-8, and 9-12. One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions. Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space. Judges Needed NASA and Future Engineers are seeking volunteers to help judge the thousands of contest entries anticipated from around the country. U.S. residents older than 18 who are interested in volunteering approximately three hours should register to judge at the Future Engineers website . The Power to Explore Student Challenge is funded by the NASA Science Mission Directorate and operates out of the Radioisotope Power Systems Program under the Research and Technology Mission Directorate. Future Engineers administers the challenge through a contract with the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. To learn more about the challenge, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/power-to-explore Eighteen-year-old Thomas Lui of Ridgewood, New Jersey; nine-year-old Rainie Lin of Lexington, Kentucky; and twelve-year-old Aadya Karthik of Seattle, Washington, winners of the 2024 Power to Explore Student Challenge explore an Apollo capsule at NASA Glenn’s Visitor Center at the Great Lakes Science Center, as a part of their prize trip to Cleveland. Photo Credit: NASA / Dave Lam

article.explanation:
**TITULAR: APOD: 24 de noviembre de 2026 – Batalla de galaxias en el Grupo NGC 7771**  
**CATEGORÍA: espacio**

El Grupo NGC 7771, ubicado a casi 200 millones de años luz en la constelación de Pegaso, es el escenario de una intensa interacción entre galaxias. En esta "batalla" cósmica, se observa cómo las galaxias NGC 7771 y NGC 7769, junto a otras más pequeñas, se acercan repetidamente, lo que podría llevar a su eventual fusión en una sola galaxia masiva.

La imagen destacada muestra anillos y remolinos de estrellas, evidencias de encuentros gravitacionales previos. NGC 7771, una galaxia espiral barrada de aproximadamente 75,000 años luz de diámetro, se encuentra en la parte inferior derecha de la imagen, mientras que NGC 7769, casi del mismo tamaño, ocupa la parte superior izquierda.

Este proceso de fusión galáctica, que se desarrolla a lo largo de miles de millones de años, es un fenómeno común en la evolución de las galaxias. Estudiar estas interacciones no solo enriquece nuestro conocimiento sobre el universo, sino que también ofrece pistas sobre el futuro encuentro entre nuestra Vía Láctea y la galaxia de Andrómeda.
article.image_headline: Se observó una colisión de galaxias en el Grupo NGC 7771, crucial para entender la evolución galáctica.
article.original_title: APOD: 2026 November 24 – Galaxies Battle in the NGC 7771 Group
article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 24 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Galaxies Battle in the NGC 7771 Group Explanation: After this galaxy battle, only one galaxy will remain. Already visible in the featured picture are rings and faint star swirls from previous gravitational encounters . Known collectively as the NGC 7771 Group , these galaxies lie almost 200 million light-years away toward the high-flying constellation Pegasus . The largest galaxy, barred spiral NGC 7771 on the lower right, is itself about 75,000 light-years across, and the galaxy on the upper left is spiral NGC 7769 , which is almost as large. As these and other smaller galaxies make repeated close passages, they will all likely merge into one very large galaxy. Playing out over billions of years, the merger process is understood to be a normal part of the evolution of galaxies . Studying galaxy clashes like this helps humanity to better understand the possible merger between our own Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies. 🌎 SISMONAUTA | CIENCIA ESPACIAL

Se observó una colisión de galaxias en el Grupo NGC 7771, crucial para entender la evolución galáctica.

CATEGORÍA: espacio El Grupo NGC 7771, ubicado a casi 200 millones de años luz en la constelación de Pegaso, es el escenario de una intensa interacción entre galaxias. En esta "batalla" cósmica, se observa cómo las galaxias NGC 7771 y NGC 7769, junto a otras más pequeñas, se acercan repetidamente, lo que podría llevar a su eventual fusión en una sola galaxia masiva. La imagen destacada muestra anillos y remolinos de estrellas, evidencias de encuentros gravitacionales previos. NGC 7771, una galaxia espiral barrada de aproximadamente 75,000 años luz de diámetro, se encuentra en la parte inferior derecha de la imagen, mientras que NGC 7769, casi del mismo tamaño, ocupa la parte superior izquierda. Este proceso de fusión galáctica, que se desarrolla a lo largo de miles de millones de años, es un fenómeno común en la evolución de las galaxias. Estudiar estas interacciones no solo enriquece nuestro conocimiento sobre el universo, sino que también ofrece pistas sobre el futuro encuentro entre nuestra Vía Láctea y la galaxia de Andrómeda.

article.description: Los científicos pueden haber explicado finalmente por qué más de mil millones de años de la historia geológica de la Tierra están ausentes en las rocas de todo el mundo. Nuevas investigaciones sugieren que corrientes poderosas en el interior del planeta elevaron y bajaron lentamente continentes enteros, permitiendo que la erosión borrara vastas extensiones de historia geológica antes de que fueran enterradas y preservadas.
article.explanation:
**Más de mil millones de años de la historia de la Tierra desaparecieron. Los científicos podrían saber por fin por qué.**

Investigaciones recientes han arrojado luz sobre el misterio de la Gran Inconformidad, un fenómeno geológico que ha dejado un vacío de más de mil millones de años en algunas formaciones rocosas de la Tierra. Un estudio liderado por un candidato a doctorado de la Universidad de Wollongong sugiere que este vacío podría explicarse por el movimiento lento de los continentes, impulsado por fuerzas profundas en el interior del planeta.

Los científicos han observado que, en diversas partes del mundo, rocas sedimentarias del período Cámbrico descansan directamente sobre rocas cristalinas mucho más antiguas, lo que indica la ausencia de capas geológicas intermedias. Este fenómeno ha sido documentado en lugares como el Gran Cañón en Estados Unidos y en regiones de Europa, Australia, África y Asia.

El estudio propone que la convección del manto terrestre, un proceso que provoca el levantamiento y hundimiento de grandes áreas de la superficie terrestre, podría ser responsable de la erosión que eliminó estas capas de roca. A medida que los continentes se elevaban, la erosión podría haber desgastado su superficie, y posteriormente, al hundirse, nuevos sedimentos se acumularon sobre las rocas expuestas, preservando así el límite geológico que observamos hoy.
