article.description: El agujero de ozono de la Antártica se expandió hasta alcanzar su séptimo mayor tamaño registrado
article.explanation:
**La NASA revela que el agujero de ozono de la Tierra ha crecido a un tamaño no visto en una década**

Recientes observaciones de la NASA y NOAA indican que el agujero de ozono sobre la Antártida alcanzó su máxima extensión en 2026, convirtiéndose en uno de los más grandes registrados en los últimos años. Este fenómeno se atribuye a un polar vortex excepcionalmente fuerte, que ha permitido que la depleción de ozono se extienda más allá de lo habitual.

El agujero alcanzó su tamaño máximo el 18 de septiembre, cubriendo aproximadamente 10.5 millones de millas cuadradas. Aunque este aumento es notable, los científicos subrayan que los esfuerzos internacionales para reducir sustancias químicas dañinas han evitado que el agujero sea aún más grande. Se estima que, sin estas medidas, el área afectada podría haber sido de 1 a 2 millones de millas cuadradas mayor.

A pesar de la expansión del agujero, los datos sugieren que la capa de ozono de la Tierra sigue en proceso de recuperación, con proyecciones que indican una sanación completa para la década de 2070. Este avance se debe en gran parte al Protocolo de Montreal, que ha llevado a una reducción significativa de los compuestos que destruyen el ozono. La situación actual resalta la importancia de la cooperación internacional en la protección del medio ambiente.

The composition of its dust provides clues to the structure of Cassiopeia A’s original star. Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A). Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets. This high-resolution, mid-infrared observation from Webb reveals new details that are helping astronomers chronicle the structure and evolution of Cas A’s original star. The Webb data supports a scenario in which the interior of the star underwent a dramatic change, possibly just hours before its demise. These results published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal Letters . Image: Dust In Cassiopeia A (MIRI Image) NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A. The composition of its dust provides clues to the structure of Cassiopeia A’s original star. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Stars begin their lives as large clouds of mostly hydrogen gas and cosmic dust called molecular clouds. Eventually, gravity causes these molecular clouds to collapse, the material heats up, and protostars — infant stars — form. Under the constant pressure of gravity, hydrogen within a protostar begins to fuse into helium, which marks the point where protostars evolve into full-fledged stars like our Sun. As hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats until helium begins to fuse into heavier elements. This process repeats as stars like Cas A’s original star evolve, with increasingly heavier elements fusing in the core (eventually stopping at iron) and lighter elements fusing in surrounding layers. This leads to multiple shells of elements that provide a record of a star’s evolutionary history. When a star goes supernova, these elements are scattered into the surrounding space, where some of them condense to form dust grains, which can clump together. By studying and mapping the composition of these individual, solar-system-sized dust clumps in Cas A, Webb found evidence of a shell merger, a process in which the layers inside a star mix before the explosion. “Material within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion,” said Tea Temim, lead author of the study and research scientist from Columbia University in New York. “So, for example, the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merge together and change the structure of the star significantly. And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion in the ejecta of a supernova remnant.” Image: Dust In Cassiopeia A, North Up (MIRI) NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A. The composition of its dust provides clues to the structure of Cassiopeia A’s original star. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) For the researchers to know where to look with Webb, they also leveraged data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope. Although it couldn’t resolve the minute details of the region during its observation , Spitzer identified three specific regions to observe with Webb’s keen eye. Two of the targets were inside Cas A’s reverse-shocked region, where an inward-moving shock wave collides with debris thrown outward by the supernova. Webb observed that the ejecta in one of the two contained mostly silica dust, while the other was dominated by carbon dust. The third target was the “ Green Monster ,” a structure first discovered by Webb, which was found to be rich in complex magnesium silicates. Unlike the other two regions, the Green Monster originated from material the star shed before it exploded, rather than from the supernova’s ejecta. Image: Dust in Cassiopeia A (Spitzer and Webb) NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope observed the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, helping to identify key regions that NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope later examined. Webb’s higher resolution provides finer details into the chemistry of the remnant’s dust. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI), Alyssa Pagan (STScI) Building on the X-ray observations of NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the JAXA-led XRISM , Webb mapped the dust composition of Cas A across the entire remnant, providing crucial insight into the shell merger phenomenon. Together, these observations indicate that the merger was underway very shortly before the supernova explosion. “With Webb, the vast improvement in being able to resolve at the individual clump level helps us do more sophisticated dust chemistry,” said Dan Milisavljevic, associate professor and co-author of the study from Purdue University in West Lafayette, Indiana. “As a result, we can tie the explosion back to the makeup of the progenitor star hundreds of years afterward. It’s telling us about what was happening, we think, in the hours leading up to core collapse. Understanding this process is essential to explaining which elements the supernova explosion will release into the galaxy and how those elements enrich future generations of stars and planets.” The dust map from Webb also reveals that the merger signatures are present throughout much of the supernova remnant. These efforts provide a new method for other astronomers who want to infer characteristics about an originating star’s structure by using the dust of a supernova remnant. The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency). article.explanation:
**El Sol desató una tormenta monstruosa. La Tierra podría haberla empeorado.**

En mayo de 2024, una tormenta solar extraordinaria provocó auroras brillantes en regiones del mundo donde estos fenómenos son poco comunes. Este evento, conocido como la "tormenta de Gannon", se caracterizó por una intensa perturbación en la magnetosfera terrestre, la cual fue medida por primera vez de manera directa. 

Los científicos observaron que, a diferencia de lo esperado, las partículas del viento solar contribuyeron muy poco a la corriente anular de la Tierra. En cambio, los iones provenientes de la atmósfera terrestre dominaron la composición de esta corriente, lo que sugiere que la atmósfera podría tener un papel más significativo en la severidad de las tormentas geomagnéticas de lo que se pensaba anteriormente. Este hallazgo fue posible gracias a las mediciones del satélite japonés Arase, que detectó que aproximadamente el 85% de los iones eran oxígeno de la ionosfera terrestre.

Las implicaciones de estos resultados son importantes, ya que las tormentas geomagnéticas pueden afectar satélites, sistemas de navegación y redes eléctricas. Comprender cómo se desarrollan estas tormentas es crucial para mejorar las predicciones y mitigar sus efectos en la tecnología moderna.

article.description: Earth is approximately 4.5 billion years old, according to estimates. However, rocks dating back to the planet's earliest days are extremely rare. Hence the excitement over the discovery in northern China of some of the oldest known rocks on Earth, dating back 3.95 billion years. And one of the reasons for all the attention is that they're revealing new clues about how Earth's crust formed and evolved.

De ahí la emoción por el descubrimiento en el norte de China de algunas de las rocas más antiguas conocidas en la Tierra, que datan de hace 3.95 mil millones de años. Y una de las razones de toda la atención es que están revelando nuevas pistas sobre cómo se formó y evolucionó la corteza terrestre.

article.explanation:
**TITULAR: NASA realiza la más reciente prueba del motor RS-25 en apoyo a las futuras misiones Artemis.**
**CATEGORÍA: espacio**

La NASA concretó una prueba de encendido estático del motor RS-25 número 10001 en el Centro Espacial Stennis, Mississippi. El ensayo, realizado el 18 de noviembre de 2026, consistió en activar este motor de desarrollo durante 200 segundos, cumpliendo con la duración que los equipos técnicos habían planificado originalmente.

Aunque esta unidad específica no se utilizará en vuelos reales, los datos obtenidos por la agencia y la empresa L3Harris Technologies son cruciales. La información capturada permitirá optimizar el rendimiento y la fiabilidad de los propulsores que integrarán el cohete SLS en las futuras etapas del programa Artemis.

Estos avances son clave para la misión Artemis IV, prevista para 2028, cuyo objetivo es llevar astronautas al Polo Sur lunar. Cada lanzamiento del SLS emplea cuatro motores RS-25 que generan dos millones de libras de empuje combinado. Con esto, la NASA busca establecer una presencia humana permanente en la superficie lunar y preparar el camino para las primeras misiones tripuladas hacia Marte.

NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Nov. 18 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Test teams fired the developmental engine for the planned duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds). While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability for future Artemis missions. For the Artemis IV Moon landing mission in 2028, the SLS rocket will launch astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This mission will be a key step in the agency’s broader goals to explore the lunar South Pole, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars. For each Artemis mission, four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket. All RS-25 engines are tested and proven flightworthy at NASA Stennis prior to use. Tests are conducted by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris, and Nova Space Solutions. Learn more about Artemis

article.explanation:
**Observatorio de siete naves espaciales para estudiar el universo de plasma**

La Agencia Espacial Europea (ESA) ha seleccionado el Plasma Observatory como su próxima misión de clase media. Este innovador proyecto contará con siete naves espaciales que, por primera vez, rastrearán cómo la energía del Sol se desplaza a través del escudo magnético de la Tierra, abarcando diferentes escalas de distancia y tiempo.

El plasma, que constituye el 99% del universo visible, es fundamental para entender fenómenos cósmicos como las tormentas solares y las auroras. Según la ESA, esta misión permitirá profundizar en cómo nuestro planeta interactúa con el plasma que lo rodea, ofreciendo una visión más detallada que nunca. La directora de ciencia de la ESA, Carole Mundell, destacó que el Plasma Observatory llevará el liderazgo europeo en heliophysics hacia la próxima década.

Las mediciones simultáneas de campos magnéticos y partículas en múltiples ubicaciones permitirán conectar eventos pequeños y rápidos con cambios más grandes en la magnetosfera. Esto proporcionará una comprensión más completa de la física subyacente a estas interacciones, tanto en nuestro sistema solar como en otros contextos cósmicos. La misión está prevista para ser lanzada a finales de la próxima década, marcando un avance significativo en la exploración del plasma.

article.description: Tsunamis triggered by volcanic eruptions are poorly understood because of the complex dynamics governing how falling rocks and ash interact with seawater to generate waves. As a result, it is difficult to anticipate whether a volcanic flow will trigger a tsunami and, if so, how big it will be. Researchers have used laboratory experiments to study this process, but little is known about how well these models mimic reality.
article.explanation: Los tsunamis provocados por erupciones volcánicas son poco comprendidos debido a la compleja dinámica que rige cómo las rocas y la ceniza que caen interactúan con el agua de mar para generar olas. Como resultado, es difícil anticipar si un flujo volcánico desencadenará un tsunami y, de ser así, cuán grande será. Los investigadores han utilizado experimentos de laboratorio para estudiar este proceso, pero se sabe poco sobre qué tan bien estos modelos imitan la realidad.

article.original_title: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation
article.source_body: Illustration of a future lunar vehicle that could potentially be powered by NASA-funded research, now under way, to develop an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module. Elementium Materials Inc. Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.S. space economy. NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed funding. This early-stage research and development work will tackle an array of topics, including those related to Artemis and the establishment of a U.S. Moon Base . Selected projects include next-generation battery solutions, robotic systems with sensing capabilities for the extreme lunar environment, and tools to prepare for construction of critical infrastructure, such as lunar landing pads. NASA’s SBIR/STTR program provides support for entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses to advance and commercialize technologies that can advance the agency’s missions. Working with the program, a company’s path toward commercialization or infusion into NASA missions occurs in phases. The latest awards involved two of these phases. The new Phase I contracts will receive up to $225,000 each to establish the merit and feasibility of their proposed innovation. A portion of the projects selected are STTR awards, provided to small businesses partnered with research institutions. The Phase II awards, with 98 contracts valued at up to $1.3 million each, will continue work begun in Phase I projects selected in 2025, targeting demonstration and delivery of the innovative technologies. Following are a few examples of research supported through these recent awards: Bringing Power to Moon and Mars An SBIR Phase II award for Opterus Research and Development Inc. supports a project focused on bringing power to the surface of the Moon and Mars by developing a modular system of rollable solar arrays. The arrays can be handled robotically, are compatible with various support structures, and work even in dusty surface conditions. The technology could be scaled up to 50 kilowatts, and it could provide a reliable power source to help both NASA and commercial space companies develop infrastructure on the Moon . Rovers With Reach: Vision and Tactile Sensing in Robotic Arm This SBIR Phase I award, led by Intelligent Fiber Optic Systems Corporation, aims to help lunar rovers perform complex tasks independently on the Moon. The firm’s 10-foot, extendable robotic arm can both “see” and has a sense of touch, combining a camera with sensors to detect and measure surface textures, contact forces, and temperature. The technology could help automate many lunar surface tasks, such as cleaning solar panels, positioning habitat structures, and collecting scientific samples from hard-to-reach locations. On Earth, the same instrumented robotic arms could be used to inspect and repair power lines, nuclear reactors, or other infrastructure in hazardous environments. Cold-Friendly Battery for Long Lunar Night Elementium Materials Inc., selected for an SBIR Phase I award, is developing an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module for space applications and cold-climate uses on Earth. The technology can operate down to minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit without active heating, reducing the need for heaters and insulating layers to work on the Moon. With the space and mass that’s saved, NASA missions can launch other tools and science experiments, instead. This battery technology could help keep rovers, habitats, and other infrastructure running through the frigid, 14-day lunar night and potentially on Mars. Prepare for Landing — Repeatedly — on Moon A collaboration between Slate Geotechnical Consultants Inc. and the Colorado School of Mines will evaluate two approaches to preparing lunar regolith for repeated lunar landings, so that routine mission activities can have sturdy, reusable landing pads. Without such pads, the force generated by a rocket can blast out loose, gravel-like regolith from the surface, throw up dust, or create craters, potentially damaging spacecraft and nearby infrastructure. The project, supported by an STTR Phase I award, will also investigate ways to use rovers to repair and maintain future lunar landing pads. Complete lists of the selected proposals are available on the SBIR/STTR program’s website: Phase I: 2026 NASA SBIR Appendix A Phase I 2026 NASA SBIR Appendix B Phase I 2026 NASA STTR Appendix B Phase I Phase II: 2025 NASA SBIR Phase II NASA’s SBIR/STTR program is part of the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate and is managed by NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley.

article.explanation:
**De contratista a funcionario público: La NASA le da la bienvenida a Jim Mirandy**

Jim Mirandy, especialista en aseguramiento de calidad en el Centro Espacial Stennis de la NASA, ha hecho la transición de contratista a funcionario público. Esta decisión forma parte de una directiva de la agencia para fortalecer las competencias técnicas dentro de su personal civil. Tras 30 años como contratista, Mirandy ahora desempeña un papel crucial en la misión de la NASA de devolver a los astronautas estadounidenses a la Luna a través del programa Artemis.

Mirandy ha sido fundamental en la implementación de protocolos de seguridad y en la formación de clases de entrenamiento en alta presión y criogénico. Su experiencia específica en el centro garantiza que las pruebas de propulsión se realicen con los más altos estándares de seguridad y calidad. Además, su trabajo incluye investigar incidentes y liderar programas de protección voluntaria.

Desde su infancia en Titusville, Florida, donde su padre trabajaba en la NASA, Mirandy ha estado vinculado al mundo espacial. Su trayectoria profesional comenzó en el Michoud Assembly Facility, donde su habilidad para resolver problemas lo llevó a enfocarse en la seguridad y la calidad. Su compromiso con la mejora continua y la seguridad de sus colegas es evidente en cada aspecto de su trabajo.

article.original_title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jim Mirandy
article.source_body: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Jim Mirandy, quality assurance specialist at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, poses for a photograph at the High Pressure Gas Facility on Nov. 10, 2026. Mirandy is now a NASA civil servant at Stennis as part of the administrator’s directive to strengthen technical core competencies within the civil service workforce. NASA/Danny Nowlin The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life. Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making. Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA. “Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.” His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through the Artemis program and ensure American leadership in space. By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards. As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe. Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center. Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis. “My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. They took the time to explain the test stands and other systems and how they worked.” A knack for fixing things helped launch Mirandy’s career at Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. He started working hands-on as a mechanic on the Space Shuttle External Tank. When an unexpected incident occurred in a production cell, Mirandy stepped up to help the operations and safety team resolve the issue. This moment shifted his career trajectory into safety and quality. Mirandy found his way to NASA Stennis and brought an understanding of systems and operations with him. A resident of Bay St. Louis and a graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, Mirandy is motivated by helping people, keeping them safe, and improving processes. “Your reward for working safely today is tomorrow,” said Mirandy. article.description: La NASA publicará las primeras imágenes de su Telescopio Espacial Nancy Grace Roman durante una transmisión en vivo desde
article.explanation:
**NASA invita a la prensa y al público a ver las primeras imágenes del telescopio Roman**

La NASA ha anunciado que el telescopio espacial Nancy Grace Roman revelará sus primeras imágenes durante una transmisión en vivo el 7 de diciembre, en el marco de la reunión anual de la Unión Geofísica Americana (AGU) en San Francisco. Este evento se llevará a cabo a las 3:30 p.m. EST y mostrará las capacidades científicas únicas del telescopio, que se propone explorar temas fundamentales como la energía oscura, la materia oscura y los exoplanetas.

Antes de la transmisión, se realizarán actividades para la prensa, incluyendo una vista previa de las imágenes a las 12 p.m. y una charla con el administrador de la NASA, Jared Isaacman, a las 2:45 p.m. Se espera que los medios registrados puedan participar en entrevistas posteriores al evento.

El telescopio Roman, lanzado el 30 de agosto, ha comenzado su viaje hacia su órbita final y está en proceso de calibración. Con su amplio campo de visión y capacidad de observación en infrarrojo, se anticipa que proporcionará datos valiosos que no solo ayudarán a entender el universo, sino que también apoyarán investigaciones en diversas áreas científicas.

article.original_title: NASA Invites Media, Public to View Roman Telescope’s First Images
article.source_body: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, seen here in the clean room at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, on Nov. 25, 2025, will explore essential questions in the areas of dark energy, exoplanets, and astrophysics. Credit: NASA/Jolearra Tshiteya NASA will release the first images from its Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope during a live stream from the American Geophysical Union (AGU) Annual Meeting in San Francisco at 3:30 p.m. EST (12:30 p.m. PST) Monday, Dec. 7. The images will showcase the unique scientific capabilities of Roman, which will soon capture deep, panoramic, never-before-seen views of the universe to explore the mysteries of dark energy, dark matter, and worlds outside our solar system. Watch the unveiling on a variety of platforms online: https://www.nasa.gov/live Roman’s first images will simultaneously post on the agency’s website . The following is a list of activities for release of the first images (all times Eastern): Dec. 7 12 p.m.: NASA will preview the images for media under embargo as part of the AGU meeting in San Francisco. To participate, either remotely or in-person, media must be registered with AGU by 8 p.m. Sunday, Dec. 6. Media can apply for AGU registration online . NASA will update this advisory later with briefing participants. The agency also will offer embargoed interviews following the conclusion of the briefing to registered media. A recording of the media briefing will be available on the AGU website after the embargo lifts at 3:30 p.m. on Dec. 7. 2:45 p.m.: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will participate in a fireside chat at the AGU meeting, moderated by journalist Alex Witze, to discuss the powerful connections between Earth and space science, the discoveries shaping our understanding of the universe, and the role NASA science plays in advancing what is possible. 3:30 p.m.: The live broadcast for the release of Roman’s images will stream through a variety of NASA platforms, in addition to AGU channels. Tuesday, Dec. 8 6 a.m. – 1 p.m.: Roman mission experts available to conduct live, remote interviews with broadcast media. More details about scheduling these interviews are forthcoming. Pixel adoption NASA invites the public to claim a corner of the universe with one of Roman’s select first images . When Roman reveals its first images, each pixel will represent a unique piece of the cosmos. Once the image is revealed, participants can look up their personal pixel and receive a digital trading card with key information they can share with NASA social accounts. Roman community events Get involved by hosting your own event for the reveal of Roman’s first images. Roman launched Aug. 30 from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, beginning a three-month, million-mile trip to its final orbit at the Sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2. During that journey, Roman has undergone a commissioning process where its systems are turned on, adjusted, calibrated, and prepared to conduct science. Roman will use its large field of view and crisp infrared vision to study vast swaths of the sky and probe deeply into cosmic history. In addition to helping scientists explore dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets, Roman’s surveys will support a broad range of research extending far beyond the mission’s main science goals. The mission also will feature a cutting-edge coronagraph technology demonstration to directly image planets around other stars. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is managed at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, with participation by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California; Caltech/IPAC in Pasadena, California; the Space Telescope Science Institute; and a science team comprised of scientists from various research institutions. The primary industrial partners are BAE Systems, Inc.; L3Harris Technologies; and Teledyne Scientific & Imaging. Stay connected with the mission and share your experience with Roman’s first images on social media. article.explanation:
**NASA realizará vuelos a baja altitud sobre tierras agrícolas de Texas**

NASA llevará a cabo vuelos de investigación a baja altitud sobre tierras agrícolas cercanas a Amarillo, Texas, desde el 22 de octubre hasta el 2 de noviembre de 2026. Estos vuelos utilizarán un avión Dynamic Aviation A200 para medir las emisiones gaseosas y de partículas provenientes de las operaciones de alimentación animal.

La misión, denominada FarmFlux, tiene como objetivo estudiar las emisiones agrícolas, un aspecto importante y poco investigado de los sistemas terrestres y atmosféricos de la Tierra. Durante la misión, se desplegarán más de una docena de sensores para medir contaminantes como ozono, metano, amoníaco y partículas, así como su interacción con la atmósfera.

La iniciativa es liderada conjuntamente por el Centro de Vuelo Espacial Goddard de NASA, la Universidad Estatal de Colorado y la Universidad de Boston. Además, se han programado vuelos de investigación adicionales con un avión P-3 Orion de NASA entre marzo y julio de 2027, centrados en tierras de cultivo en el Medio Oeste y el Valle Central de California. Estos esfuerzos buscan mejorar la comprensión de las emisiones agrícolas y su impacto en el medio ambiente.

article.original_title: NASA to Conduct Low-Altitude Flights Over Texas Farmland
article.source_body: Editor’s Note: This article was originally published on Oct. 15, 2026, and has been updated to correct the location and update the duration of the flight deployment. A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Amarillo, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 2. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations. A photo of the Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft, which will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Amarillo, Texas, to measure emissions in October and November 2026. Dynamic Aviation Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy more than a dozen sensors to measure ozone, methane, ammonia, particulates, and other pollutants rising from crop lands and livestock farms and their interaction with the Earth’s atmosphere. The mission is jointly led by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland; Colorado State University; and Boston University. Additional low-altitude research flights with a NASA P-3 Orion aircraft are scheduled for the March to July 2027 growing season in the Midwest and California’s Central Valley with a focus on cropland. For more information about the FarmFlux mission, visit: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/evs-4/farm-flux/ By Sharon Teitelbaum NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley

article.explanation: **TITULAR: APOD: 18 de noviembre de 2026 – Una llamarada solar de clase M** El 18 de noviembre de 2026, el Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) presenta una imagen de la cromosfera solar, capturada durante una llamarada solar de clase M1 ocurrida el 14 de mayo de 2025. Esta llamarada, moderadamente brillante en rayos X, es un fenómeno que se origina en la atmósfera del Sol, donde la temperatura aumenta debido a la energía generada por campos magnéticos en movimiento. Las llamaradas solares, como la M1, pueden provocar interrupciones en las comunicaciones de radio en los polos de la Tierra y generar tormentas de radiación menores que representan un riesgo para los astronautas en el espacio. Aunque no son las más potentes, su monitoreo es crucial para la seguridad de las actividades espaciales y terrestres. Agencias como NASA y NOAA están constantemente vigilando la actividad solar para predecir y gestionar estos eventos, asegurando así la protección de los seres humanos tanto en la Tierra como en el espacio. La comprensión de estos fenómenos es esencial para mitigar sus efectos y avanzar en la exploración espacial.

article.original_title: APOD: 2026 November 18 – An M-class Solar Flare
article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 18 – An… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Medium-Sized Solar Flare Explanation: What a flare for the chromatic ! Today’s image captures a piece of the Sun ’s chromosphere , the layer of the Sun ’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises . Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core ? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap , releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare . The H-alpha filter used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was classified as an M1 based on GOES observations , meaning it was moderately bright in X-rays . M-class flares can cause radio blackouts at Earth’s poles and minor radiation storms that can harm astronauts. They aren’t even the most powerful flares ! NASA, NOAA , and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space. article.explanation:
**Equipos definen la arquitectura de la misión para el SR-1 Freedom de la NASA**

La NASA ha completado una revisión crucial del diseño de su misión Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, la primera nave espacial propulsada por fisión que viajará más allá de la órbita terrestre. Este hito se alcanzó en octubre, cuando expertos de la agencia, el Departamento de Energía de EE. UU. y la industria se reunieron en el Centro de Investigación Glenn en Cleveland.

El SR-1, programado para lanzarse a finales de 2028, utilizará energía nuclear y solar para entregar la cápsula SkyFall a Marte. Esta cápsula llevará tres helicópteros de nueva generación que explorarán la geología y el clima marciano, buscando signos de hielo subsuperficial. La misión es un paso significativo hacia la exploración más profunda del sistema solar, ya que se espera que la energía nuclear permita misiones de larga duración en entornos donde la luz solar es limitada.

Entre las decisiones clave, se ha optado por un brazo más corto para separar el reactor del cuerpo principal de la nave, lo que simplificará su diseño y reducirá el peso. Además, se están realizando mejoras en el sistema de blindaje y en la integración del reactor, garantizando la protección necesaria para los componentes electrónicos y la carga útil. 

Con estos avances, el SR-1 Freedom se perfila como un pionero en el transporte espacial propulsado por energía nuclear, sentando las bases para futuras misiones de exploración.

article.original_title: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom
article.source_body: 5 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, cruises past Mars in this artist’s concept, demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space. Credit: NASA/Jonathan North NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time. Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland for a major SR-1 mission design review in October. Several key decisions were made, propelling the mission from an early concept toward a defined spacecraft design. “SR-1 marks a pivotal step in how we travel through the solar system,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “This mission will be the first freight run on the railroad of the solar system, and the decisions we’re making now are laying the tracks for every nuclear-powered spacecraft that follows.” Planned for launch in late 2028, SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall , a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars. Once deployed, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history, explore new terrain, and search for signs of subsurface ice. As NASA prepares for more ambitious exploration missions, future spacecraft and surface operations will require significantly more power than current systems can provide, particularly in environments where sunlight is limited or unavailable. SR-1 will demonstrate how fission power can enable long-duration missions, pave the way for reliable surface power systems to support NASA’s future Moon Base , and enable exploration deeper into the solar system. Key design decisions The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft design has evolved since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first introduced the concept in March at the agency’s Ignition event, where leadership shared plans to develop a fission-powered spacecraft in time for the next Mars launch window. One significant change is to use a shorter boom than the one shown in early illustrations. The boom separates the reactor from the spacecraft’s main body, known as the Power and Propulsion Element. The shorter boom will reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design. Planned for launch in late 2028, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall to Mars. This infographic explains the components of the spacecraft. Credit: NASA/David Lam NASA and DOE experts also determined that improvements in shielding and spacecraft design will allow the reactor to operate closer to the rest of the spacecraft. This will simplify integration while maintaining the radiation protection needed for spacecraft electronics and the SkyFall payload. Teams are continuing to evaluate other key design features, including the number of radiator panels on SR-1, output power levels of its nuclear power module , and how long its reactor will operate. These decisions will help shape the final spacecraft design and ensure it meets mission objectives. In addition, the team is modifying the spacecraft’s Power and Propulsion Element by updating its communications system for the journey to Mars. SR-1 Freedom will use larger X-band antenna dishes to send data across deep space back to Earth. Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule. NASA awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the spacecraft’s nuclear power module. The system will remove excess heat generated by the spacecraft’s nuclear power system, allowing it to operate safely and efficiently. The lab is working with the company Advanced Cooling Technologies as a key strategic commercial partner for providing the critical heat pipe and composite radiator technologies that will enable the system to meet the demanding mission requirements. Awarded under the Aerospace Research, Development, and Engineering Support II contract, the contract action ensures the Applied Physics Laboratory team will design, build, test, and evaluate the system, along with producing the hardware needed for flight. The heat rejection system is a key part of demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in space and will help lay the groundwork and industrial production foundation for future high-power nuclear systems used in deep space exploration. Updated mission profile Along with the spacecraft design, teams have defined the mission timeline and planned operations. After launch and once the spacecraft has left Earth orbit, SR-1 Freedom will activate and gradually increase reactor power. The reactor system will operate for an initial period of time before shutting down. During this period, the spacecraft will collect and send performance data back to Earth. Solar arrays will then provide power as it cruises to Mars. NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, cruises past Mars in this artist’s concept, demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space. Credit: NASA After delivering SkyFall to Martian orbit, SR-1 Freedom will restart its fission reactor, collecting additional data on the spacecraft’s performance in deep space. “By refining the design and advancing this architecture, we’re not just building a spacecraft, we’re establishing the foundation for a new era of reliable, efficient transport beyond Earth orbit,” Sinacore said. “What we learn from SR-1 Freedom will shape the future of exploration for decades to come.” With key design decisions advancing and teams across NASA, DOE, and industry working together, SR-1 Freedom is moving toward its 2028 launch goal. The mission will demonstrate new capabilities for nuclear-powered transportation and help establish the foundation for future exploration beyond Earth. To learn more about NASA’s efforts in nuclear power in space, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/space-nuclear

Equipos definen la arquitectura de la misión para el SR-1 Freedom de la NASA La NASA ha completado una revisión crucial del diseño de su misión Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, la primera nave espacial propulsada por fisión que viajará más allá de la órbita terrestre. Este hito se alcanzó en octubre, cuando expertos de la agencia, el Departamento de Energía de EE. UU. y la industria se reunieron en el Centro de Investigación Glenn en Cleveland. El SR-1, programado para lanzarse a finales de 2028, utilizará energía nuclear y solar para entregar la cápsula SkyFall a Marte. Esta cápsula llevará tres helicópteros de nueva generación que explorarán la geología y el clima marciano, buscando signos de hielo subsuperficial. La misión es un paso significativo hacia la exploración más profunda del sistema solar, ya que se espera que la energía nuclear permita misiones de larga duración en entornos donde la luz solar es limitada. Entre las decisiones clave, se ha optado por un brazo más corto para separar el reactor del cuerpo principal de la nave, lo que simplificará su diseño y reducirá el peso. Además, se están realizando mejoras en el sistema de blindaje y en la integración del reactor, garantizando la protección necesaria para los componentes electrónicos y la carga útil. Con estos avances, el SR-1 Freedom se perfila como un pionero en el transporte espacial propulsado por energía nuclear, sentando las bases para futuras misiones de exploración.

article.explanation:
**¿Qué es la base lunar?**

La base lunar es el primer puesto avanzado de la humanidad en la Luna, donde astronautas vivirán, trabajarán y explorarán. Se ubicará en el polo sur lunar, una región elegida por sus condiciones de iluminación únicas y su potencial para descubrimientos científicos. En esta área, algunas zonas reciben luz solar durante períodos prolongados, lo que podría ser útil para generar energía solar, mientras que otras permanecen en la sombra y podrían contener depósitos de agua helada.

La construcción de la base lunar se llevará a cabo en tres fases. Actualmente, se está realizando la primera fase, que incluye el envío de misiones robóticas para explorar el polo sur y probar nuevas tecnologías. La segunda fase, programada para 2029-2032, se centrará en establecer la infraestructura a largo plazo, como sistemas de energía y transporte. Finalmente, en la tercera fase, se ensamblará un puesto avanzado permanente donde los astronautas podrán vivir y trabajar por períodos extendidos.

La base lunar no solo es un hito en la exploración espacial, sino que también servirá como un laboratorio para preparar futuras misiones a Marte.

article.original_title: What Is the Moon Base?
article.source_body: 7 Min Read What Is the Moon Base? This article is for students. NASA is returning astronauts to the Moon – and this time they will spend more time on the lunar surface. The Moon Base is humanity’s first lunar outpost . It will be a place where astronauts live, work, and explore. Artist’s concept depicting astronauts, habitats, rovers, power systems, and cargo operations supporting sustained human activities at the Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. NASA ______________________________________________________________________ Words to Know outpost: a station or base located in a remote, distant place infrastructure: the basic framework and systems that make up a larger building or organization terrain: the physical features, shape, and layout of the surface of a piece of land, including its slope and elevation regolith : the layer of loose, fragmented rock and mineral dust covering most of the lunar surface ______________________________________________________________________ Where Will the Moon Base Be Built? The Moon Base will be built in the lunar South Pole region. This area was selected for its unique lighting conditions and potential for scientific discovery. Near the lunar South Pole, the Sun stays low on the horizon. Some areas can receive extended periods of sunlight. Other areas stay in shadows for long periods of time. In some craters, sunlight may never reach the surface at all. Areas that receive extended sunlight could be good for generating solar power. Longer sunlight hours are also good for navigating and exploring. Areas that remain in shadows are some of the coldest areas on the Moon. In these locations, scientists hope to find deposits of frozen water ice. When Will the Moon Base Be Constructed? The Moon Base will be constructed in three phases. Each phase will build on what is learned along the way. Phase One is taking place right now. Over the next few years, NASA and its partners will send robotic missions to explore the lunar South Pole region. They will test new technologies and practice landing on the Moon. This phase will include multiple different landers and lunar terrain vehicles. These missions will conduct science experiments and look for the best locations for building the Moon Base. Phase Two is planned for 2029-2032. During this period, NASA will begin setting up long-term infrastructure . This includes things like power systems, cargo transportation, and communications hardware. These components will be set up across multiple locations. This will allow for future expansion of the Moon Base. During Phase Three, NASA will begin assembling a permanent lunar outpost. This is where astronauts will be able to live and work for extended periods. Habitats, power and communication systems, and transportation will all come together to grow Moon Base. An artist’s concept design of a lunar terrain vehicle. NASA What Are the Different Components of the Moon Base? Crewed and robotic lunar rovers will play an important role in the development of the Moon Base. These rovers will test out technologies, transport astronauts, map terrain , and more. Let’s learn about a few of the rovers being built as part of the Moon Base. NASA’s VIPER (Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover) is fully built. It is being tested at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. In 2027, it will launch to the Moon from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Its mission will be to explore permanently shadowed craters to look for water and other resources. It will travel more than 15 miles, collecting data and analyzing the lunar soil. NASA’s PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration) is a nuclear-powered rover. It is being built from existing hardware that was created for NASA’s Mars rover missions. PROMISE will look for resources – like potential water ice – on and below the lunar surface. It will carry multiple science instruments, including several that are also on VIPER. The mission is targeted to launch by late 2028. Lunar terrain vehicles (LTVs) will launch to the lunar South Pole region by 2028. These crewed vehicles will be driven by astronauts during missions to the Moon. This will allow the crew to explore larger areas and gather geology samples. When astronauts are not on the Moon, the LTVs will be remotely operated from Earth. They will map the lunar surface and collect data about the extreme environment in the region. In addition to rovers, NASA’s MoonFall mission will send a group of propulsive drones to the Moon. They will land near the lunar South Pole by 2028. The drones will descend to the lunar surface independently. They will operate separately over the course of a single lunar day (about 14 Earth days). They will use high-definition cameras to map hard-to-reach terrain. This data will help NASA select potential Artemis landing sites. What Are the Challenges of Building on the Moon? The lunar South Pole region is an extreme environment. The Moon doesn’t have any noticeable atmosphere. This means temperatures can reach more than 130°F (54°C) in sunlit areas. And it can be as cold as -334°F (-203°C) inside permanently shadowed craters. This can be very dangerous for astronauts. But it is also a challenge for designing infrastructure and hardware. Navigating the uneven lunar surface can be difficult. The South Pole region of the Moon has steep slopes, ridges, rocks, and deep craters. Shackleton Crater is more than twice as deep as the Grand Canyon. Detailed mapping and robotic exploration will help NASA identify safe landing areas and plan routes for astronauts and rovers. The lunar surface is covered with regolith . This layer of rocky material is the result of meteoroid impacts. Since there is no wind or rain to cause erosion on the lunar surface, regolith particles have sharp edges. This means regolith can quickly wear down spacesuits and equipment. It can be particularly irritating to skin and dangerous if inhaled. Precautions must be taken to keep regolith and lunar dust out of areas where astronauts live. How Will the Moon Base Prepare Us for Future Missions? The Moon Base is an important step in learning how to live and work on another world. What we learn on the lunar surface by testing new landing techniques, construction methods, and exploration technologies will help prepare for human missions to Mars. Exploration geologist Angela Garcia wears a spacesuit prototype while testing science operation techniques for future Artemis missions to the lunar surface. NASA Career Corner Here are a few examples of the careers that are making NASA’s Moon Base plans possible: Space tire engineer: The rovers being designed as part of the Moon Base need to have special tires. Engineers must consider the lack of atmosphere, extreme temperature, and rocky terrain when designing tires to drive long distances on the Moon. A career in engineering demands a strong understanding of math and complex problem-solving. An advanced college degree is usually required. Click here to see a space tire engineer in action. Exploration geologist : These scientists study rocks and minerals on Earth and throughout the solar system. They look at geological processes to see how erosion and harsh environments can change terrain. For Moon Base, they’re helping to select locations to explore on the lunar surface. And they’re helping train the astronauts who will land and gather samples. This career requires strong observational skills and usually requires an advanced college degree. Click here to see what it’s like being an exploration geologist at NASA. Manufacturing technician: Turning designs into reality takes skilled technicians. Fabrication and assembly of robotic equipment and spacecraft parts requires precise calculations. Being able to follow intricate instructions is key. Trade school training and skills such as operating forklifts and heavy machinery may be required. Instrument technician : These experts install, calibrate, and maintain sensors and control systems. They troubleshoot issues that might come up with delicate systems and equipment. This career path often starts with an apprenticeship or hands-on training alongside experienced technicians. An associate’s degree is often required. Click here to see some of the testing completed on one of the Moon Base landers. article.description: Over the past 800,000 years, Earth's history has been marked by dramatic shifts in climate, swinging from warm periods to cold, when large ice sheets covered much of the Northern Hemisphere and sea ice greatly expanded. The transition between the two climates is paced by the Earth's orbit with respect to the sun, but changes in the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2), a greenhouse gas, also affect global temperatures. By understanding how CO2 is exchanged between the atmosphere and the ocean, scientists hope to apply that knowledge to future climate scenarios.

La transición entre los dos climas está determinada por la órbita de la Tierra con respecto al sol, pero los cambios en la cantidad de dióxido de carbono (CO2), un gas de efecto invernadero, también afectan las temperaturas globales. **TITULAR: Fotos de astronautas de Gemini inspiraron programa temprano de observación de la Tierra**

En noviembre de 1966, durante la misión Gemini XII, los astronautas James Lovell y Buzz Aldrin registraron imágenes del Mar Rojo y el valle del Nilo. Este último vuelo del programa Gemini no solo cumplió objetivos técnicos espaciales, sino que demostró el valor científico de observar la superficie terrestre desde la órbita.

Las fotografías capturadas por la tripulación fueron fundamentales para que científicos e instituciones justificaran la creación de un programa satelital dedicado. William T. Pecora, entonces director del Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos, fue un defensor clave de esta iniciativa tras notar la utilidad de los registros visuales obtenidos en las misiones Mercury y Gemini para el estudio de recursos

article.original_title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
article.source_body: NASA astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. captured this image of the area surrounding the Red Sea and Nile river valley on November 14, 1966, during their four-day mission in space. Gemini XII was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini Program. NASA Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII , the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program. In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of a different field of exploration, observing Earth from space. The photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface. Their images helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program. One of strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, the director of the United States Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971. In a 1969 statement, Pecora noted that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite (EROS) program he championed, and which later paved the way for Landsat , was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.” For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have provided invaluable data used around the world to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health, land use, and countless other changes to our planet. article.explanation:
**Descripción general de la misión CRS-25 de Northrop Grumman de la NASA**

La misión CRS-25 de Northrop Grumman, parte de los Servicios Comerciales de Reabastecimiento de la NASA, tiene como objetivo entregar aproximadamente 11,000 libras de suministros y experimentos científicos a la Estación Espacial Internacional (EEI). Esta será la tercera misión del Cygnus XL, una versión más grande y capaz del vehículo espacial de la compañía, que se lanzará a bordo de un cohete Falcon 9 de SpaceX desde la Estación de la Fuerza Espacial de Cabo Cañaveral en Florida.

Entre los experimentos que se enviarán se encuentran investigaciones sobre el tratamiento de la pérdida muscular, el desarrollo de nanomateriales para la medicina regenerativa y el monitoreo de la radiación en entornos espaciales. Por ejemplo, el estudio "Cardinal Muscle 2.0" busca explorar tratamientos para la atrofia muscular, un problema que afecta tanto a astronautas como a personas mayores en la Tierra.

Además, la misión incluye el desarrollo de tecnologías de soldadura robótica en el espacio, lo que podría facilitar la construcción de estructuras grandes en futuras misiones de exploración. Estos avances no solo son cruciales para la investigación espacial, sino que también tienen el potencial de mejorar tratamientos médicos en la Tierra.

article.original_title: NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission Overview
article.source_body: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft. The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following arrival to the station, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 to grapple the spacecraft before ground controllers robotically install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will launch on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket to deliver research and supplies to the International Space Station. Credit: NASA NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will deliver approximately 11,000 pounds of research and supplies to the International Space Station. Credit: NASA NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Mission 25 will launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Credit: NASA NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 spacecraft is named in honor of NASA astronaut James “Jim” A. Lovell Jr. Lovell flew four missions, including Gemini VII, Gemini XII, Apollo 8, and the Apollo 13 mission around the Moon. Credit: NASA NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney will be on duty during the Cygnus spacecraft’s approach and rendezvous. Watkins will be at the controls of the Canadarm2 robotic arm, ready to capture Cygnus as Delaney monitors the spacecraft’s arrival. Credit: NASA Science highlights In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments aimed at improving drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis treatment, predicting cancer spread, advancing treatments for muscle loss, improving radiation sensing, and supporting food production for future long-duration missions. This research includes: Cardinal Muscle 2.0 Preflight image of the Biocell bioreactor system used to maintain engineered muscle tissue samples as part of the Advancing Therapeutic Treatment of Sarcopenia (Cardinal Muscle 2.0) investigation. Aboard the International Space Station, this investigation tests the effects of potential therapeutics on human muscle cell cultures. The research may help accelerate development of treatments for age-related muscle loss on Earth and support astronaut health during long-duration missions. Credit: Palo Alto Veteran’s Institute for Research Cardinal Muscle 2.0 uses the microgravity environment to explore potential treatments for muscle loss. Muscle atrophy and strength loss experienced by astronauts after spaceflight share many features with age-related muscle decline on Earth and occur more rapidly in microgravity without exercise. Researchers will use a muscle tissue model to test different Food and Drug Administration-approved drugs used to treat other conditions can be repurposed to prevent or reduce muscle loss. DNA NANO B A confocal microscope image shows a human cartilage cell, with its nucleus stained in blue, following delivery of Janus Base Nanoparticles (JBNp) and the subsequent release of bioactive mRNA (pink) that was translated into function protein (green). Biomimetic Fabrication of Multi-Functional DNA-Inspired Nanomaterials via Controlled Self-assembly in Space (DNA Nano Therapeutics-Mission 2) continues prior research on in-space manufacturing of nanomaterials that mimic DNA and have applications for vaccines and regenerative medicine. Credit: University of Connecticut The DNA Nano B investigation uses microgravity to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles designed to deliver medicine into dense tissues, such as cartilage and solid tumors. Microgravity may enable more uniform particle assembly, helping researchers refine production methods. The results could advance targeted treatments for cancer and osteoarthritis on Earth. ARES Preflight image of an Active Radiation Environment Sensor (ARES) unit undergoing ground testing in a thermal vacuum chamber. This investigation monitors radiation in habitable spacecraft environments and has exposure awareness and warning capabilities for Human Landing System crews. Testing aboard the International Space Station helps researchers validate the technology for future exploration missions. Credit: NASA/HHPC The Active Radiation Environment Sensor ( ARES ) will test a small radiation monitoring device to support future Artemis program and lunar missions. The system is designed to integrate with spacecraft systems and provide real-time radiation monitoring inside crew living areas. The results could inform radiation monitoring strategies and crew safety measures for future exploration missions. ENCAPSULATE-1 Preflight image of colorectal microtumors grown within Encapsulate’s biochip. The investigation, Encapsulate nVasive: Unraveling the Enigma of Metastasis – Flight 1, or Encapsulate-1, grows copies of patients’ tumor samples aboard the International Space Station to study how cancer cells move and interact in microgravity. Results may help researchers develop further testing to predict a patient’s risk of metastasis and support more personalized cancer treatments. Credit: Encapsulate Inc. Encapsulate-1 uses miniature replicas of patients’ tumors to study how cancer cells move, invade surrounding tissues, and potentially spread. Researchers aim to develop a space-based diagnostic tool that could predict cancer progression months or even years in advance, improving early detection and treatment decisions for patients on Earth. OHALO III Preflight image of Utah State University’s OHALO III module with a variety of plants growing from the Utah Re-usable Root Modules. This facility aims to validate plant water delivery, volume optimization, and advance knowledge on crop production, which could inform design decisions for future plant systems on deep space missions. Credit: NASA KSC Ohalo III is a new plant growth facility designed to help food crop production on future long-duration missions. The mostly automated system uses innovative water recovery and air exchange technologies to grow a variety of crops. This research could help lead to better food production methods to keep crew healthy and fed on future exploration missions, including those to Mars. Technology demonstration The upcoming JOINS demonstration inside the Bishop Airlock will perform autonomous robotic welding in space. JOINS will test two distinct approaches: laser beam welding and friction stir welding. Laser beam welding uses a high-precision laser to melt and fuse materials together. Friction stir welding uses a rotating tool to stir the metals together, and that friction generates enough heat to soften the materials. JOINS will perform these welding approaches on two different materials: aluminum and stainless-steel. Credit: Lockheed Martin JOining demonstrations IN-Space (JOINS) will mature technologies that allow robotic systems to join materials directly in space. In-space joining could enable large structures to be assembled and integrated after launch rather than being constrained by the size and volume of a launch vehicle. These capabilities may be needed to build and repair large infrastructure, such as structures that will to support future exploration under Moon Base . Testing technologies in space helps validate their performance in unique environmental conditions, matures their readiness for operational use, reduces technical risk, and builds confidence for future mission applications. Mission hardware Additional supplies being flown to the space station include: Crew quarter blankets and covers to replace old units on station. Hatch seal covers to be installed on U.S. segment hatch seals. A modified toilet pretreat hose needed to operate the universal pretreat concentrate tank in the Universal Waste Management System toilet. Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer specific spacewalk tools to be used during upcoming spacewalks. Anomaly Gas Analyzer batteries required to power various sensors on space station. To learn more about NASA’s work in low Earth orbit, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/international-space-station

La misión CRS-25 de Northrop Grumman entregará 11,000 libras de suministros y experimentos a la Estación Espacial Internacional.

La misión CRS-25 de Northrop Grumman, parte de los Servicios Comerciales de Reabastecimiento de la NASA, tiene como objetivo entregar aproximadamente 11,000 libras de suministros y experimentos científicos a la Estación Espacial Internacional (EEI). Esta será la tercera misión del Cygnus XL, una versión más grande y capaz del vehículo espacial de la compañía, que se lanzará a bordo de un cohete Falcon 9 de SpaceX desde la Estación de la Fuerza Espacial de Cabo Cañaveral en Florida. Entre los experimentos que se enviarán se encuentran investigaciones sobre el tratamiento de la pérdida muscular, el desarrollo de nanomateriales para la medicina regenerativa y el monitoreo de la radiación en entornos espaciales. Por ejemplo, el estudio "Cardinal Muscle 2.0" busca explorar tratamientos para la atrofia muscular, un problema que afecta tanto a astronautas como a personas mayores en la Tierra. Además, la misión incluye el desarrollo de tecnologías de soldadura robótica en el espacio, lo que podría facilitar la construcción de estructuras grandes en futuras misiones de exploración. Estos avances no solo son cruciales para la investigación espacial, sino que también tienen el potencial de mejorar tratamientos médicos en la Tierra.

La calificación es la mejor opinión de auditoría posible, certificando que los estados financieros de la NASA se ajustan a los Principios de Contabilidad Generalmente Aceptados para agencias federales y presentan con precisión la posición financiera de la agencia. “Nuestra responsabilidad […]
article.explanation:
**NASA recibe decimosexta opinión de auditoría financiera "limpia" consecutiva**

NASA ha logrado, por décimo sexta vez consecutiva, una opinión de auditoría externa "limpia" sobre sus estados financieros del año fiscal 2026. Este reconocimiento, el más alto en auditoría, asegura que los informes financieros de la agencia cumplen con los Principios de Contabilidad Generalmente Aceptados para agencias federales y reflejan con precisión su situación financiera.

El administrador de NASA, Jared Isaacman, destacó la importancia de ser responsables en la gestión de los recursos públicos y subrayó que esta auditoría limpia es un testimonio del compromiso de la agencia con la rendición de cuentas financieras. El informe financiero de 2026 también resalta los avances en las misiones de NASA, incluyendo el exitoso vuelo de prueba de la misión Artemis II, que marcó hitos significativos en la exploración espacial.

Además, se anunciaron iniciativas transformadoras para fortalecer el liderazgo estadounidense en el espacio, como la construcción de una base lunar y el lanzamiento anticipado del telescopio espacial Nancy Grace Roman, destinado a estudiar fenómenos como la materia oscura y la energía oscura. Estos logros reflejan el compromiso de NASA con la transparencia y la innovación en la exploración espacial.

article.original_title: NASA Receives 16th Consecutive ‘Clean’ Financial Audit Opinion
article.source_body: Credit: NASA For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements. The rating is the best possible audit opinion, certifying that NASA’s financial statements conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies and accurately present the agency’s financial position. “Our responsibility at NASA is to be disciplined stewards of the resources entrusted to us by the American people while delivering on the missions they expect from this agency,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Our 16th consecutive clean audit reflects a long record of financial accountability, and we intend to pair that discipline with the urgency and execution required to take on the near-impossible missions ahead.” The 2026 Agency Financial Report provides key financial and performance information and demonstrates the agency’s commitment to transparency in the use of American taxpayers’ dollars. In addition, the 2026 report presents progress during the past year, and spotlights advancements in NASA missions, objectives, and workforce development with these financial resources. In fiscal year 2026 (FY 2026), NASA’s 10-day Artemis II mission successfully accomplished a test flight around the Moon with four crew members, delivering major human spaceflight milestones, such as the record‑breaking distance astronauts have traveled from Earth and global public engagement. NASA also announced a series of transformative agencywide initiatives designed to advance American leadership in space, including plans to build a Moon Base, which will be humanity’s first lunar outpost, and a place where astronauts will live, work, and explore near the Moon’s South Pole. NASA’s science advancements in FY 2026 included launching the agency’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, ahead of schedule, to study dark matter, dark energy, planets outside our solar system, as well as exploration of everything from nearby stars to distant galaxies. NASA’s experimental X-59 quiet supersonic aircraft achieved a major milestone when it flew faster than the speed of sound for the first time. The agency also: launched NASA Force with the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, a talent track designed to recruit and deploy the nation’s top engineers and technologists to support America’s space program; announced an agencywide realignment to increase mission focus; and welcomed additional Artemis Accords signatories committing to the safe, transparent, and responsible exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond. For more information on NASA’s budget, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/budget -end- George Alderman / Jennifer Dooren Headquarters, Washington 202-358-1600 george.a.alderman@nasa.gov / jennifer.m.dooren@nasa.gov Share Details Last Updated Nov 16, 2026 Location NASA Headquarters Related Terms Office of the Chief Financial Officer (OCFO) Budget & Annual Reports
