Créditos: Purpose Entertainment/Shanna Lockwood Empleados e invitados del Centro Espacial Johnson de NASA celebran el 65º aniversario del centro en el Parque de Recepción Lunar en Houston el 11 de noviembre. NASA/Robert Markowitz Durante 65 años, el Centro Espacial Johnson de NASA en Houston ha ayudado a dar forma al vuelo espacial humano, desde las misiones Gemini que demostraron las técnicas de encuentro y acoplamiento necesarias para Apollo hasta la investigación realizada a bordo de la Estación Espacial Internacional, que ha apoyado una presencia humana continua durante más de 26 años. Hoy, los equipos de Johnson se están preparando para las tripulaciones y sistemas para el próximo capítulo de NASA: devolver astronautas a la superficie lunar y construir las capacidades necesarias para una presencia humana a largo plazo en la Luna.
article.image_headline: 65 años de vuelos espaciales tripulados en el NASA Johnson
article.original_title: 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson
article.source_body: 7 Min Read 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano, former NASA astronaut Russell “Rusty” Schweickart, and NASA astronauts Frank Rubio and Bob Hines appear onstage at the Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Merritt Island, Florida, on Nov. 6, 2026. Credits: Purpose Entertainment/Shanna Lockwood Employees and guests of NASA’s Johnson Space Center celebrate the center’s 65th anniversary at the Lunar Receiving Park in Houston on Nov. 19, 2026. NASA/Robert Markowitz For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years. Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and systems for NASA’s next chapter: returning astronauts to the lunar surface and building the capabilities needed for a long-term human presence at the Moon. Across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth. Johnson is home to NASA’s Orion and Moon Base programs, and its teams continue to support space station operations, astronaut training, spacecraft development, mission operations, and human health. Mercury and Gemini: Preparing for Apollo When the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, NASA had already flown two suborbital Mercury missions, with the first orbital flight just months away. Most Project Mercury activities remained at Cape Canaveral in Florida to maintain continuity, but the new Project Gemini took up residence in Houston, housed in temporary leased facilities across the city while construction of the new Clear Lake campus continued. The new Mission Control Center became NASA’s primary flight control center in June 1965, with the Gemini IV mission that included the first American spacewalk. Houston became the nerve center for American human spaceflight, overseeing the remaining eight Gemini missions before transitioning to the Apollo program. Following the tragic Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, managers, engineers, and astronauts at the Manned Spacecraft Center applied lessons learned to make the spacecraft safer and ensure the safety of its astronauts, resuming crewed missions in October 1968. Managers in Houston devised a daring plan to send Apollo 8 on a circumlunar flight. In December 1968, Apollo 8 made its historic trip around the Moon, and seven months later Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed on the lunar surface. Their first voice transmission back to Earth after their arrival began with the word “Houston.” Five more Moon landings completed the Apollo program and humanity’s first phase of lunar exploration in December 1972. Following the Moon landings, scientists at the Manned Spacecraft Center’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory conducted initial analyses of Apollo lunar samples and prepared them for researchers around the world. After the building was demolished in March 2024, the Lunar Receiving Park was dedicated to honor the laboratory’s history in 2026. Today, Johnson’s Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science ( ARES ) division continues to analyze and curate the Apollo collection at the Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility. Six of the seven Mercury astronauts pose with Manned Spacecraft Center Director Robert Gilruth outside the new center’s temporary headquarters building in Houston in March 1962. Not pictured, astronaut John Glenn, still on his postflight tour two weeks after becoming the first American to orbit the Earth aboard Friendship 7. Flight controllers work in Mission Control in Houston during the Gemini IV mission in June 1965, the first spaceflight controlled from the new center. Astronauts aboard Gemini VI photograph Gemini VII during the world’s first rendezvous mission in December 1965. The famous Earthrise photograph taken during the Apollo 8 mission around the Moon in December 1968. Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong photographs fellow crew member Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin saluting the American flag on the surface of the Moon in July 1969. Skylab and Apollo-Soyuz: Learning to Live and Work in Space Skylab, America’s first space station, ran into trouble during its launch in May 1973, losing its thermal shield, jamming one solar array and losing the other one. In less than 10 days, engineers in Houston designed and built a sun shield and generated procedures to free the jammed array, followed by the first extensive in-orbit repair activities by the first Skylab crew. The three missions lasting 28, 59, and 84 days accomplished more research than planned, demonstrated the value of humans on long-duration missions, and provided operators in mission control with round-the-clock experience monitoring long duration human spaceflights. In July 1975, after several joint training sessions in Houston and Moscow, American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts met in space for the first time during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. Approved as a project in 1972, five approach and landing tests of the space shuttle using orbiter Enterprise paved the way for the first orbital mission of Columbia in 1981. In August 1973, Skylab 3 Commander Alan Bean during one of the many spacewalks conducted during Skylab to repair and maintain the station and conduct research. Farewell view of the Skylab space station from the departing Skylab 4 crew in February 1974. The famous handshake in space took place on July 17, 1975, between Apollo Commander Thomas Stafford, top, and Soyuz Commander Aleksei Leonov. In October 1977, space shuttle Enterprise conducts its first approach and landing test with the tail cone removed. The Space Shuttle: Setting the Stage for Long-Duration Spaceflight Engineers in Houston began designs for a reuseable space plane in the late 1960s, with the space shuttle receiving formal approval in 1972. During the 1970s, Johnson Space Center put in place the training and simulation facilities that astronauts used for the life of the program. Upgrades to mission control enabled the use of the latest technologies to support ever more complex space shuttle missions. The April 1981 launch of space shuttle Columbia inaugurated a new era of reusable spacecraft. The program’s 135 missions flew 355 individuals from 16 nations. Missions included satellite deployments and retrievals, dedicated Department of Defense flights, a variety of science missions including deployment of planetary spacecraft, ferrying crews and cargo to two different space stations, and doing the heavy lifting in the assembly of the orbiting laboratory. The program recovered from the tragic losses of the Challenger and Columbia crews with renewed emphasis on crew safety. The final space shuttle mission, STS-135, closed out the 30-year program in July 2011. Space shuttle Columbia lifted off on April 12, 1981, ushering in a new era of reusable space transportation Astronaut Bruce McCandless flies the Manned Maneuvering Unit in April 1984 during the STS-41B mission. Space shuttle Atlantis docked with the Russian space station Mir in July 1995. The Hubble Space Telescope during STS-125, the final servicing mission to the orbiting observatory in May 2009. The four astronauts of STS-135, the final space shuttle mission in July 2011, stand before Atlantis at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center at the conclusion of their mission. The Space Station: 26 Years of Continuous Human Presence An Earth orbiting space station, first approved by President Ronald Reagan in 1984, underwent many modifications before taking on its current form as the International Space Station in 1993. Overall management of the program resides at Johnson. The first element launch took place in November 1998, followed one month later by the first U.S. element, the Node 1 Unity module. The first expedition crew took up residence on Nov. 2, 2000, and for more than 26 years, rotating crews of astronauts and cosmonauts have lived and worked aboard the orbiting laboratory, establishing a permanent human presence in low Earth orbit. To date, 298 individuals from 26 countries have visited the space station, conducting more than 4,000 science experiments and educational activities to enable exploration missions and improve life on Earth. Life aboard the space station depends on a global team on the ground. Crews conduct research and maintain equipment in microgravity, while Johnson teams at the Mission Control Center coordinate the agency’s station operations with international partners. Johnson’s Space Vehicle Mockup Facility supports training for NASA astronauts and international crews on station systems, science operations, and emergency procedures. At the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory, crews rehearse spacewalks around full-scale station mockups in one of the world’s largest indoor pools. Johnson’s Human Research Program also supports health investigations aboard the station, helping researchers understand how spaceflight affects the body so crews can thrive on future deep space missions. What began as a framework of modules has evolved into a springboard for international cooperation, advanced scientific research and technology demonstrations, the development of a low Earth orbit economy, and NASA’s next giant leaps in exploration. The space station continues to be a proving ground for NASA’s Artemis program and human exploration of Mars. The International Space Station as it appeared to the departing STS-106 crew in September 2000, shortly before the first expedition crew took up residence. The Expedition 1 crew of Yuri Gidzenko of Roscosmos, left, NASA astronaut William Shepherd, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergei Krikalev aboard the space station in December 2000. Departing Expedition 27 crew members aboard Soyuz TMA-20 photographed space shuttle Endeavour docked to the space station during STS-134 in May 2011. The space station is pictured from a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft by a SpaceX Crew-8 member shortly after undocking from the Harmony module’s space-facing port. Eleven members of Expedition 75 pose in the Kibo module during a change of command ceremony in October 2026. Members of the Expedition 75 flight control team monitor U.S. Spacewalk 97 from the Mission Control Center at Johnson Space Center on Aug. 18, 2026. NASA/James Blair Expedition 75 flight engineer Anil Menon captured a view of the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft during U.S. Spacewalk 98 on Aug. 25, 2026. Artemis and Moon Base: Building a Sustained Lunar Presence The Artemis II mission marked the first crewed flight of NASA’s Orion spacecraft. The four-person crew launched April 1, on a nearly 10-day trip around the Moon. At its farthest point, Orion traveled 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans had traveled before. The mission demonstrated Orion’s capabilities with astronauts aboard and tested crew operations in deep space, setting the stage for future lunar missions. Building on Artemis II, NASA’s Artemis III mission will test integrated operations in low Earth orbit between Orion and test versions of one or both commercial human landing systems under development by SpaceX and Blue Origin. Astronauts will demonstrate the rendezvous and docking capabilities needed to transfer crews between spacecraft for the lunar landing planned for Artemis IV. NASA’s Moon Base Program is planning a phased effort to support a sustained human presence near the Moon’s South Pole. The first phase will focus on robotic exploration, technology demonstrations, and preparations for future surface operations. Later phases will add infrastructure to support astronauts living and working on the Moon. Lunar terrain vehicles will help crews explore farther, transport equipment, and conduct science. At Johnson, teams are drawing on decades of experience in astronaut training, mission control, spacecraft development, and human health to prepare for these missions. From training crews for lunar operations to developing the systems that will support them, Johnson is building on 65 years of human spaceflight experience for humanity’s return to the lunar surface through the Artemis and Moon Base Programs. A full Moon is seen shining over NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) and Orion spacecraft, atop the mobile launcher in the early hours of February 1, 2026. The rocket is currently at Launch Pad 39B at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, as teams are preparing for a wet dress rehearsal to practice timelines and procedures for the launch of Artemis II. NASA/Sam Lott The Artemis II crew – (clockwise from left) Mission Specialist Christina Koch, Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen, Commander Reid Wiseman, and Pilot Victor Glover – pause for a group photo with their zero gravity indicator “Rise,” inside the Orion spacecraft on their way home from their nearly 10-day voyage around the Moon. article.description: University of Michigan researchers have developed a better way to understand why earthquakes occur and what size they might be. Currently, models that predict earthquakes only account for slipping that occurs along a main fault, activity that usually generates large earthquakes. Instead, the U-M researchers have built a model that considers not only the main fault action but also the activity of rocks that lie adjacent to the fault and become damaged during earthquake events.
article.explanation: Investigadores de la Universidad de Michigan han desarrollado una mejor manera de entender por qué ocurren los terremotos y qué tamaño podrían tener. Actualmente, los modelos que predicen terremotos solo consideran el deslizamiento que ocurre a lo largo de una falla principal, actividad que generalmente genera grandes terremotos. En cambio, los investigadores de U-M han construido un modelo que considera no solo la acción de la falla principal, sino también la actividad de las rocas que se encuentran adyacentes a la falla y que se dañan durante los eventos sísmicos.

article.description: Una erupción volcánica justo frente a la costa sureste de la isla del Pacífico ha remodelado la costa, pero no está claro cuánto tiempo sobrevivirá la nueva tierra.
article.explanation:
**Erupción extiende la playa de Iwo Jima**

Una reciente erupción volcánica en las aguas poco profundas cerca de Iwo Jima ha ampliado temporalmente las famosas playas de arena negra de la isla japonesa. La actividad volcánica comenzó a notarse a finales de octubre de 2026, cuando los sensores sísmicos registraron un aumento significativo en la actividad. Fotografías del evento fueron capturadas poco después, mostrando la magnitud de la erupción.

El 16 de noviembre, la Guardia Costera de Japón confirmó la formación de nueva tierra, que se ha conectado a la playa existente. Se estima que la erupción ha añadido aproximadamente 50 hectáreas de nueva playa, lo que representa un incremento del 1.7% en el tamaño de la isla. Esta nueva extensión de tierra se encuentra adyacente a la playa donde desembarcaron las tropas estadounidenses en 1945, durante una de las batallas más sangrientas de la historia de los Marines.

Sin embargo, la permanencia de esta nueva tierra es incierta. Investigaciones previas indican que las formaciones de tierra volcánica suelen ser rápidamente erosionadas por las olas. Expertos sugieren que, si no se inyecta lava que fortalezca el material, es probable que esta nueva extensión desaparezca en pocos meses. La vigilancia continua por parte de satélites permitirá monitorear los cambios en la zona.

article.original_title: Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s Beach
article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search October 26 November 11 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison October 26 November 11 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison October 26 November 11 Curtain Toggle 2-Up A volcanic eruption in the shallows near Iwo Jima has extended the Japanese island’s famed black sand beaches, at least temporarily. Signs of unrest began in late October 2026. On October 27, seismic sensors recorded a sharp uptick in activity, and Japan’s Meteorological Agency reported that the first photographs of the eruption were captured. Soon after, sensors on several satellites began to capture an array of observations. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured the left image on October 26, when the coast was still quiet. On November 11, Landsat 9 got its first clear view of the land the submarine volcano has built (right). A shortwave-infrared signature, a sign of the eruption’s heat, is shown in orange. A faint gray volcanic plume drifts southeast of the vent, and a streak of floating pumice stretches across the water in the same direction. A false-color backscatter radar image from the NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite offered an even earlier look at the eruption. On October 28, despite heavy cloud cover, the radar detected a large disturbance in the water in the same area that erupted in December 2023. When the clouds cleared in early November, the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors on NASA and NOAA satellites also captured signs of the ongoing eruption’s volcanic plumes and infrared signature . Japan’s Coast Guard released a report on November 16 confirming the formation of new land connected to the pre-existing beach. The eruption appears to have added roughly 50 hectares (125 acres) of new beach, about the area of 90 American football fields. That would enlarge the island by about 1.7 percent. The new land adjoins the southeast beach where American troops landed on February 19, 1945, beginning one of the bloodiest battles in the history of the U.S. Marines. The location of the eruption is no surprise to scientists. In addition to the 2023 eruption off the southeast coast, Iwo Jima had an eruption off its west coast in August 2025, said Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. How long the new land will persist remains an open question. New land created by the 2023 eruption succumbed to wave action after just a few weeks, Slayback said. New land on volcanic islands has persisted more than a decade only a handful of times in recent times, including at Capelinhos, Surtsey, McDonald Island, and Home Reef, he added. “I imagine we’ll see this new land wash away within a few months,” he said. “But we’ll have to wait and see.” Among the scientists watching closely is James Garvin, the chief scientist at Goddard and a geologist with a long-standing interest in how underwater volcanic eruptions create new islands and other landforms. Typically, tephra -dominated eruptions like this form new land that is quickly “attacked” by ocean waves and other hydrologic forces, Garvin explained. An exception is when the eruption also injects certain types of lava that “cement” the ash into stronger material. “If we do see injection of basaltic-andesitic lava within the new materials, then it’s possible the new land could follow a pattern different from what we monitored in 2023,” he said. NISAR will be especially valuable for tracking the site, Garvin said, because it makes frequent, high-resolution interferometric observations through clouds and can show whether the new land erodes, subsides, or grows. The satellite has already recorded major changes at the eruption site between October 28 and November 11 . NASA scientists will also analyze sub-meter-resolution imagery from commercial satellites through NASA’s Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition Program . These images can reveal subtle deformation features like rilles, fractures, and cracks that offer clues about the stability of the new land. Both Slayback and Garvin have studied new volcanic land before. They were part of a team that monitored new land in the Kingdom of Tonga after an eruption in the Southwest Pacific but before most of it was obliterated during the highly explosive Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha‘apai caldera collapse and eruption in January 2022. article.description: La NASA demostró con éxito tecnología diseñada para ayudar a las naves espaciales a navegar de forma autón
article.explanation: NASA ha realizado avances significativos en su experimento de navegación conocido como SPLICE (Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution), diseñado para mejorar la precisión de los aterrizajes en la Luna y Marte. Este sistema fue probado en un dron Alta-X en el Centro de Investigación de Vuelo Armstrong en California, donde demostró su capacidad para comunicarse eficazmente durante maniobras de vuelo. El SPLICE utiliza un sistema de guía avanzado que permite mapear el terreno y evaluar áreas de aterrizaje potenciales. Si el sistema determina que el área objetivo es insegura, puede redirigir el dron a un lugar más seguro. Este enfoque es crucial para las misiones futuras de NASA, ya que garantiza aterrizajes más seguros y precisos en superficies extraterrestres. Davis Adams, gerente del proyecto, destacó que esta prueba representa el resultado de casi una década de trabajo y que el sistema está listo para ser integrado en futuras misiones robóticas y tripuladas. Además, se están realizando colaboraciones con proveedores de módulos lunares para implementar SPLICE en sus plataformas, lo que podría facilitar aterrizajes suaves en la superficie lunar en misiones venideras.

article.original_title: NASA Navigation Experiment Shows Promise for Planetary Landings
article.source_body: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) An Alta-X drone flies an advanced guidance and navigation system known as the Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) experiment near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed SPLICE, which successfully communicated with the remotely piloted aircraft during hover maneuvers in flight. SPLICE will help spacecraft land precisely and detect and avoid potential hazards, which is critical for NASA missions to the Moon and to Mars. NASA/Ryan Kline NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets. An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution ( SPLICE ) guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place at Rogers Dry Lake near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. During the tests, the SPLICE payload used an advanced guidance system to map the terrain and assess potential landing areas. If the system determines the targeted landing area is unsafe, the system diverts the drone to a safer location. The system generates high-resolution digital elevation maps from light-detection and sensor data. Davis Adams, project manager, confirms that an advanced guidance and navigation system known as the Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) experiment is communicating with an Alta-X drone near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed SPLICE, which successfully communicated with the remotely piloted aircraft during hover maneuvers in flight. SPLICE will help spacecraft land precisely and detect and avoid potential hazards, which is critical for NASA missions to the Moon and to Mars. NASA/Ryan Kline Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed the SPLICE payload and partnered with specialists at NASA Armstrong to integrate, test, and fly it aboard the Alta-X drone in June and July. Those tests verified communications, data handling, telemetry, and command- control performance between the SPLICE payload and the drone to prepare for a full-scale test at Voyager Technologies in Mojave, California, later this month. “This flight test is the culmination of almost a decade of work, for the SPLICE project,” said Davis Adams, NASA project manager. “This flight raised the technology readiness level, priming it for integration into future robotic and crewed lunar flights. Validation of the guidance and navigation systems are applicable to terrestrial, lunar, and Martian descent and landing missions.” NASA has worked with a number of commercial lunar lander providers to implement iterations of SPLICE into their platforms. A number of the landers slated for upcoming Moon Base missions leverage data collected by NASA through the development of systems like SPLICE to execute soft touchdowns on the lunar surface. Justin Link, a small uncrewed aircraft pilot, left, Justin Hall, chief pilot, and Davis Adams, project manager, test an advanced guidance and navigation system known as the Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) experiment on an Alta-X drone near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed SPLICE, which successfully communicated with the remotely piloted aircraft during hover maneuvers in flight. SPLICE will help spacecraft land precisely and detect and avoid potential hazards, which is critical for NASA missions to the Moon and to Mars. NASA/Carla Thomas “We are coordinating with industry regarding the usage of the guidance system once the system is available in the NASA software catalog, currently planned for this fall,” Adams said. “Some of the companies also are evaluating the system’s navigation capabilities for precision landing applications, as well as potential extensions for autonomous surface mobility.” NASA’s Flight Opportunities project, based at NASA Armstrong, enabled flight testing of the SPLICE project early in its development that laid a foundation for it to continue advancing its technology readiness level to what it is today. Flight testing included both a descent altitude and a landing trajectory in 2019 similar to what is expected on a lunar mission and the demonstration of two NASA-developed precision landing sensor systems in 2020. article.explanation:
**APOD: 18 de noviembre de 2026 – Una fulguración solar de tamaño mediano**

El 18 de noviembre de 2026, se observó una fulguración solar de tamaño mediano, clasificada como M1, que se produjo el 14 de mayo de 2025. Este fenómeno fue capturado en una serie de imágenes que muestran la cromosfera del Sol, la capa de su atmósfera donde la temperatura aumenta a medida que se aleja del núcleo.

Las fulguraciones solares son explosiones de energía que ocurren debido a la interacción de campos magnéticos en la superficie solar. Durante este evento, se liberaron luz y partículas energéticas, lo que puede tener consecuencias en la Tierra. Las fulguraciones de clase M, aunque no son las más potentes, pueden causar apagones de radio en los polos y generar tormentas de radiación menores que pueden afectar a los astronautas en el espacio.

Agencias como NASA y NOAA monitorean constantemente la actividad solar para predecir estos eventos y proteger a los seres humanos tanto en la Tierra como en el espacio. La comprensión de estos fenómenos es crucial para mitigar sus efectos en la tecnología y la salud de los astronautas.

article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 18 – A… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Medium-Sized Solar Flare Explanation: What a flare for the chromatic ! Today’s image combines a series of images taken over ten minutes capturing the Sun ’s chromosphere , the layer of the Sun ’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises . Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core ? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap , releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare . The H-alpha filter used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was classified as an M1 based on GOES observations , meaning it was moderately bright in X-rays . M-class flares can cause radio blackouts at Earth’s poles and minor radiation storms that can harm astronauts. They aren’t even the most powerful flares ! NASA, NOAA , and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space. A medida que la NASA se prepara para misiones de larga duración en el espacio profundo […]
article.explanation:
**Desafío AVATAR Digital BPS**

El programa AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) de la NASA se centra en el estudio de los efectos de la radiación y la microgravedad en la salud humana mediante dispositivos de organ-on-a-chip. Este experimento, que se llevará a cabo en la misión Artemis II, busca generar conocimientos que puedan beneficiar tanto a astronautas en el espacio como a la población en general.

La investigación se enmarca dentro del Programa de Biología Espacial de la NASA, que examina cómo los sistemas vivos responden a los estresores únicos de la exploración espacial. Con la mirada puesta en misiones de larga duración, se hace esencial desarrollar estrategias de salud personalizadas para proteger a los miembros de la tripulación.

El desafío digital AVATAR invita a la comunidad científica a utilizar tecnologías innovadoras de gemelos digitales para acelerar el descubrimiento biológico y modelar la salud de los astronautas. Se busca crear modelos computacionales que simulen cómo responde la médula ósea a los estresores del vuelo espacial, integrando datos diversos para generar predicciones de salud personalizadas.

Este enfoque no solo promete mejorar la salud de los astronautas, sino que también podría tener implicaciones significativas para la medicina en la Tierra.

article.original_title: BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge
article.source_body: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) The AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation will use organ-on-a-chip devices, or organ chips, to study a effects of increased radiation and microgravity on human health. Artemis II AVATAR is a small experiment flying aboard Artemis II that could lead to big impacts in healthcare, both for astronauts in space and citizens on Earth. For more information on AVATAR: go.nasa.gov/4m5dGH9 The NASA Space Biology Program within the Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) Division investigates how living systems respond across the full spectrum of biological organization to advance understanding of how living systems respond to the unique stressors of space exploration—including microgravity, ionizing radiation, low magnetic fields, and elevated CO₂. As NASA prepares for long-duration deep space missions, the need to protect individual crew members with personalized, data-driven health strategies is becoming increasingly important. The original AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation, which flew aboard the Artemis II mission, marks a significant milestone: organ-on-a-chip devices constructed from the cells of actual crew members returned from a 10-day lunar flyby on April 10, 2026. AVATAR is the first demonstration of an Artemis astronaut analog using an organ-on-a-chip model to generate personalized biological insights that can inform medical kits and countermeasures for future deep space missions. Digital twins represent a key strategy for addressing these challenges. By developing individualized computational physiological models that can be iteratively refined with empirical data, these frameworks integrate environmental, physiological, and multi-omics inputs. This approach allows for the simulation and prediction of how a specific individual will respond to spaceflight stressors. The BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge invites the scientific community to apply innovative computational digital twin technologies to accelerate biological discovery, biochemical and molecular modeling, and predictions of individual astronaut health outcomes. The digital twin will be a computational model of how the AVATAR bone marrow chip responds to spaceflight stressors. The proposed digital twin frameworks must be capable of processing diverse multi-modal datasets and leverage established computational biology methods alongside modern digital twin architectures to create personalized, predictive models of astronaut physiology. These systems are expected to model each astronaut’s immune and bone marrow hematopoietic responses to spaceflight, integrating multi-modal data to generate tailored health predictions — including comparative analysis that distinguishes individual-specific effects from effects common across the crew. Proposals should also demonstrate a pathway to continuous model updating as new empirical data become available, reflecting the iterative nature of a true digital twin. Award: $150,000 in total prizes Registration Open Date: November 16, 2026 Submission Deadline: February 12, 2027 For more information including registration , rules, and eligibility, visit: https://work.crowdplat.com/challenge/bps-digital-twin-challenge

article.description: Rondas de lluvias intensas en el suroeste de EE. UU. inundaron ríos y elevaron rápidamente el segundo embalse
article.explanation:
Entre fines de octubre y principios de noviembre de 2026, una serie de tormentas extremas azotó la región de Four Corners, en el suroeste de Estados Unidos. Este fenómeno, impulsado por temperaturas oceánicas inusualmente altas y el patrón de El Niño, provocó un aumento crítico en los caudales de la zona.

Según datos satelitales de la NASA, el Embalse Navajo, ubicado entre Nuevo México y Colorado, elevó su nivel en casi 18 metros en apenas siete semanas. Para el 7 de noviembre, el reservorio alcanzó el 108% de su capacidad promedio, su punto más alto desde agosto de 2019. Esto contrasta drásticamente con el 60% registrado en septiembre del mismo año.

Las consecuencias fueron duales. Por un lado, el desborde de ríos como el San Juan causó inundaciones severas en localidades como Pagosa Springs, obligando a evacuaciones y dañando infraestructura. Por otro lado, los expertos documentaron el fin de la sequía de corto plazo en el suroeste y la Gran Cuenca, aunque la escasez hídrica de largo plazo aún persiste en diversos sectores del territorio.

article.original_title: Water Surges Into Navajo Reservoir
article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Water Surges Into Navajo… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Back-to-back extreme rain events inundated the Four Corners region of the U.S. Southwest in late October and early November 2026. The storms alleviated short-term drought conditions in the Southwest but caused river levels to spike to record or near-record levels in places, triggering damaging floods. One effect of the heavy rains detected by satellites was the rapid rise of water levels in Navajo Reservoir. The change is visible in the images above, acquired on September 20 (left) and November 7 (right) with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 . In that time, the lake in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado rose by nearly 60 feet (18 meters), according to data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. (Note that the Bureau of Reclamation decreased releases from Navajo Dam on September 16 and 17.) On November 7, the reservoir stood at its highest level since August 2019 and at 108 percent of the average capacity for that date. That contrasts with September 20, when it held just 60 percent of its average capacity. Due to snow drought across the West in winter 2025-26, the lake saw relatively little growth in the spring, when snowmelt often raises water levels. The San Juan, Piedra, and other rivers swelled with runoff amid the wet weather. Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a town along the San Juan River about 40 miles (64 kilometers) northeast of the lake, was especially hard-hit by flooding. In the first round of rain, 5.05 inches (12.8 centimeters) fell in the town, and on October 23 the river reached major flood stage . After more rain, the river spiked again on November 1, this time nearly to the record level set in 1911 during a devastating flood . Officials issued evacuation orders, and responders rescued dozens of people, according to news reports , while water inundated streets and damaged property. Heavy rain and flooding have been widespread across southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico in recent weeks. From early September through early November, precipitation totals were 2 to 4 times the average throughout the Four Corners region—an area beset by long-term drought that was exacerbated by snow drought and high temperatures in 2026. Though the downpours posed hazards to communities along many rivers, they did provide drought relief throughout the region. Weekly U.S. Drought Monitor maps, derived from a suite of satellite data products and ground-based observations, have indicated improvements to drought conditions due to the fall storms. The group’s November 3 summary noted that “short-term drought has ended for the Southwest and Great Basin,” although long-term drought persists in places. Wet weather in the Southwest is often associated with El Niño events, when the segment of the jet stream flowing eastward near the equatorial Pacific tends to strengthen. Experts noted that the low-pressure system delivering the heavy rainfall in autumn 2026 was at a low latitude for the time of year and drew energy from unusually high ocean temperatures. El Niño patterns—like the one currently underway —can increase the likelihood of moisture-laden storms being steered across the Southwest interior. article.description: Un estudio pionero con drones ha revelado una división sorprendente en el destino de los pingüinos de cresta erecta
article.explanation:
**CATEGORIA: oceanos**

Investigadores de la Universidad de Otago han revelado una desconcertante realidad dual para el pingüino de cresta erecta en Nueva Zelanda. Tras realizar censos con drones entre 2022 y 2024, el estudio determinó que, mientras la población en las pequeñas islas Bounty se ha mantenido estable por 25 años, la de las islas Antípodas ha caído más de un 40% desde 1995.

Esta "paradoja de Schrödinger" se explica por presiones ambientales divergentes. En las Antípodas, el declive se vincula a tormentas más intensas y al aumento de la depredación por parte de skúas, aves que aprovechan la reducción de las colonias para atacar huevos y polluelos. Además, estos pingüinos migran distancias mayores hacia zonas polares, a diferencia de los ejemplares de las Bounty, que permanecen en aguas más protegidas.

La principal consecuencia es un dilema para su conservación. Si se promedian ambas poblaciones, el estatus de la especie podría mejorar artificialmente a "Vulnerable". Los científicos advierten que esto generaría una falsa sensación de seguridad, ocultando la crisis en las Antípodas y dejando a las colonias estables de las Bounty desprotegidas frente a amenazas como la pesca industrial.

article.description: Profundamente bajo el Océano Pacífico, los científicos han descubierto pequeños ecosistemas ocultos dentro de rocas ricas en metales que tardan millones de años en formarse. Los investigadores examinaron 244 nódulos y encontraron más de 4,100 animales viviendo en sus grietas y cavidades, incluyendo comunidades únicas diferentes a las del barro del fondo marino circundante. Estos notables hábitats en miniatura podrían estar ahora amenazados por la minería en aguas profundas en busca de metales valiosos.
article.explanation:
**Ecosistema oculto: Científicos descubren 245 animales viviendo dentro de una sola roca en el fondo del mar**

Investigadores han revelado un ecosistema sorprendente en el fondo del océano Pacífico, donde 245 animales habitan dentro de una única roca, conocida como nódulo polimetálico. Estos nódulos, formados por óxidos de hierro y manganeso, ofrecen refugio a organismos microscópicos en sus grietas y cavidades, creando hábitats en un entorno predominantemente blando.

El estudio, liderado por la ecóloga marina Dr. Tanja Stratmann, identificó un total de 4,139 animales en 244 nódulos, con un promedio de 17 por nódulo. Aunque la cantidad de vida en los nódulos es menor que en el sedimento circundante, su diversidad es notable. Las comunidades de animales dentro de los nódulos son genéticamente distintas de las que habitan en el sedimento, lo que sugiere que estos nódulos son hábitats especializados.

La investigación también plantea preocupaciones sobre el impacto de la minería en el fondo marino, ya que la extracción de nódulos podría llevar a la pérdida irreversible de biodiversidad. Los nódulos requieren millones de años para formarse, lo que significa que su eliminación podría resultar en la extinción de especies que dependen de estos hábitats únicos. La protección de estos ecosistemas ocultos es crucial para la conservación marina.

Las comunidades de animales dentro de los nódulos son genéticamente distintas de las que habitan en el sedimento, lo que sugiere que estos nódulos son hábitats especializados. La investigación también plantea preocupaciones sobre el impacto de la minería en el fondo marino, ya que la extracción de nódulos podría llevar a la pérdida irreversible de biodiversidad. Los nódulos requieren millones de años para formarse, lo que significa que su eliminación podría resultar en la extinción de especies que dependen de estos hábitats únicos. La protección de estos ecosistemas ocultos es crucial para la conservación marina.

article.explanation:
**Datos de la NASA confirman la primera fusión estelar en su tipo**

Investigadores han documentado un evento sin precedentes en la Andrómeda, donde un sistema estelar binario, apodado Bao, experimentó una fusión estelar. Este descubrimiento fue posible gracias a observaciones del Telescopio Espacial James Webb de la NASA, que proporcionó evidencia crucial sobre lo que ocurrió antes, durante y después de la fusión.

El evento comenzó cuando una estrella, ligeramente menos masiva que el Sol, se acercó y se fusionó con una supergigante. Este proceso, que se desarrolló en un corto período de siete años, contrasta con otros casos de fusiones estelares que requieren miles de órbitas. Los investigadores notaron un aumento inusual en el brillo de Bao en 2023, lo que llevó a un seguimiento intensivo que culminó en una erupción en 2025.

Los datos del Webb permitieron a los científicos caracterizar la evolución de las estrellas y medir la masa eyectada durante la fusión. Este hallazgo no solo amplía nuestra comprensión de las fusiones estelares, sino que también establece un nuevo camino para futuras investigaciones en astrofísica, especialmente con el próximo telescopio Nancy Grace Roman.

article.original_title: NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger
article.source_body: Explore Webb Science James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) NASA Data Clinches… Webb News Latest News Latest Images Webb’s Blog Awards X (offsite – login reqd) Instagram (offsite – login reqd) Facebook (offsite- login reqd) Youtube (offsite) Overview About Who is James Webb? Fact Sheet Impacts+Benefits FAQ Webb Timeline Science Overview and Goals Early Universe Galaxies Over Time Star Lifecycle Other Worlds Science/Engineering Explainers Observatory Overview Launch Deployment Orbit Mirrors Sunshield Instruments & ISIM Module Instrument: NIRCam Instrument: MIRI Instrument: NIRSpec Instrument: FGS/NIRISS Optical Telescope Element Backplane Spacecraft Bus Webb vs Hubble -> Multimedia About Webb Images Images Videos Products & Activities Podcasts Webb Image Sonifications What is Webb Observing? 3d Webb in 3d Solar System Webb’s First Images Team International Team People Of Webb More For the Media For Scientists For Educators For Fun/Learning 7 Min Read NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy. Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially “rejuvenated” star Bao. Their NASA-funded discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground. “Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,” said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature published Wednesday and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. “However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars’ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope’s data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.” Image: AT 2025abao in the Andromeda Galaxy In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler Before their transformation, the two stars spent millennia placidly orbiting one another as a binary pair. But once the smaller star came into contact with the surface of the giant star, their “unification” happened after only seven orbits (about seven years). Other known binary star mergers, featuring two smaller stars, occurred after thousands of orbits. “We thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,” said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. “One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!” “When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect — a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao’s data,” said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. “As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star’s outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.” This is the beginning of a high-stakes showdown some binary stars go through, known as a common envelope evolution. The gas between the stars at this stage is known as a common envelope because its outer layer is shared between them. In this system, the primary star engulfed the smaller star and the companion plummeted, spiraling through the envelope as it was robbed of orbital energy by drag. While Webb’s data proved the stars merged, a merger wasn’t the only possible outcome for this system. In other systems, both stars survive the process — shedding a lot of mass along the way, but remaining independent in tight orbits. Over time, such surviving pairs can transform into neutron stars and black holes , explode as supernovae , produce ripples in space-time known as gravitational waves , and create millisecond pulsars . Hitting “replay” The team reconstructed what happened to Bao by updating their ongoing simulations. They found the model that matched Webb’s mid-infrared observations, which detailed the dust shed by the more massive primary star over centuries. The team concluded that prior to the eruption, Bao’s primary star dwarfed the Sun: It was seven times as massive, 350 times the radius, and 18,000 times brighter — making “Big Bao” an appropriate nickname. “It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,” said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations. Their modeling resulted in the first mass estimate for the smaller, now demolished, companion. Compared to our Sun, they found that “Little Bao” was likely less massive (about 0.7 solar masses), with a slightly smaller radius and fainter. After revealing the masses of the pair, the model showed there might be leftover energy for Little Bao to “flee” the scene. However, further analysis determined that Little Bao was dragged into Big Bao’s core. Their encounter was “almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star,” De said. What does the new star — now simply Bao — look like today? Only future observations will identify how its “heft” settles. Image: Andromeda Star Merger (Artist’s Concept) Top to bottom, left to right: In this artist’s concept, the stars are surrounded by a dust shell pre-merger; the stars brightened and the companion star’s orbit began to slow as the larger star engulfed it; the eruption occurred; dust freely expands at the poles after the merger. Illustration: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia) Reconstructing what happened While Webb’s data allowed the team to measure how much mass was ejected during this process and how efficient the process of common envelope evolution was, Karambelkar’s team also used observations that span ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light from several telescopes to watch the events, often as they unfolded. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.) Bao first caught the team’s attention in February 2023, when they saw an unusual variable star in data from NASA’s retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission. Before 2018, the object had a consistent luminosity. Observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) in September 2024 showed that Bao was not only beginning to brighten, but also spew dust. When NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) serendipitously saw Bao fade rapidly in visible light and brighten in infrared light during a routine survey in July 2025, the researchers knew it was an indicator of unusual activity. The Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption on Oct. 17, 2025, watching the stars rapidly brighten and radically heat up. In November 2025, the team received fast-turn observations from NASA’s now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab’s Gemini North telescope in Hawaii. Webb’s observations were taken on Dec. 24, 2025, as part of a just-in-time Director’s Discretionary Time program . New path for future research The team’s analysis of Bao, formally known as AT 2025abao, offers an approach to reconstructing the events: They conducted their analysis and made observations of the stars’ merger in real time. That allowed them to measure how efficient common envelope evolution is. In other cases, astronomers have worked to carefully reverse-engineer events that may have happened hundreds or even millions of years ago. The new finding comes about just as NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to conduct vast publicly available surveys . Its Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey will yield a huge number of new transient events that could benefit from similar analyses. “There’s going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead,” Karambelkar said. This work is funded in part by a grant from NASA’s Astrophysics Data Analysis Program. The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency). article.explanation: **TITULAR: APOD: 21 de noviembre de 2026 – El Neptuno de la Voyager** El 21 de noviembre de 2026, la imagen destacada del día en el Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) presenta una impresionante vista de Neptuno, capturada por la sonda Voyager 2. Este encuentro cercano, que tuvo lugar el 25 de agosto de 1989, marcó un hito en la exploración del sistema solar, ya que Voyager 2 es la única nave que ha visitado este distante planeta gigante de hielo. La imagen muestra a Neptuno y su mayor luna, Tritón, como delgadas medias lunas iluminadas por el Sol. Se pueden observar nubes cirros y una banda oscura que rodea la región polar sur del planeta, así como un vórtice nuboso sobre el polo. Además, se destacan los anillos tenues de Neptuno, que fueron fotografiados por primera vez durante el sobrevuelo de Voyager. En la actualidad, Voyager 2 continúa su viaje en el espacio interestelar, proporcionando datos valiosos sobre el entorno más allá de nuestro sistema solar. Esta imagen no solo es un recordatorio de los logros de la exploración espacial, sino también de la belleza y complejidad de nuestro universo.

article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 21 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Voyager’s Neptune Explanation: Cruising through the outer solar system, the Voyager 2 spacecraft made its closest approach to Neptune on August 25, 1989, the only spacecraft to visit the most distant ice giant planet . Based on the images recorded during its close encounter and in the following days, this inspired composited scene covers the dim outer planet, largest moon Triton , and faint system of rings. From just beyond Neptune’s orbit, the interplanetary perspective looks back toward the Sun, capturing the planet and Triton as thin sunlit crescents . Cirrus clouds and a dark band circle Neptune’s south polar region, with a cloudy vortex above the pole itself . Parts of the very faint ring system along with the three bright ring arcs were first imaged by Voyager during the fly-by, though the faintest segments are modeled in this composited picture. Spanning 7.5 degrees, the background starfield is composed from sky survey data centered on the constellation Camelopardalis, corresponding to the outbound Voyager’s view of the magnificent Neptunian system . Still cruising in 2026, the Voyager 2 spacecraft is now in interstellar space . **El James Webb revela los secretos de la formación estelar en NGC 7129**

La NASA ha publicado una detallada imagen de la región de formación estelar NGC 7129, captada en luz infrarroja por el Telescopio Espacial James Webb. Esta tecnología permite atravesar el polvo opaco que usualmente bloquea la visión en luz convencional, revelando el complejo nacimiento de nuevos astros.

El proceso comienza cuando la gravedad agrupa masivas cantidades de gas. En la captura se distinguen dos zonas clave: a la izquierda, entre nubes de color dorado, se ubican estrellas jóvenes relativamente maduras. A la derecha, en la región rojiza, se encuentran astros en etapas más tempranas de su evolución.

La estructura filamentosa del gas rojo es consecuencia de los potentes chorros y vientos emitidos por las estrellas en formación. Estos fenómenos, que incluso pueden derivar en explosiones, moldean el entorno galáctico de manera dinámica.

article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 16 – NGC… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb Explanation: How do stars form? To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light . Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds — and some then explode . Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image , with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right — in the red region. Jets and wind s likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when. article.description: Un notable descubrimiento fósil en Colombia está desafiando la forma en que los científicos entienden los principales cambios evolutivos en la historia de la Tierra. Los investigadores descubrieron un ecosistema marino antiguo increíblemente diverso donde reptiles gigantes, tiburones y otras criaturas prosperaron mientras grupos evolutivos más antiguos se acercaban a la extinción y otros más nuevos emergían. Llaman a este patrón previamente no reconocido una "Inflexión Biótica", sugiriendo que transformaciones importantes en la vida pueden ocurrir sin extinciones masivas.
article.explanation:
**Un océano antiguo lleno de depredadores gigantes revela un giro sorprendente en la evolución**

Investigaciones en la Formación Paja, en Colombia, han desvelado un capítulo fascinante de la historia evolutiva de la Tierra. Un equipo de científicos de la Universidad McGill y el Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas ha encontrado fósiles que indican que grupos de animales antiguos, en peligro de extinción, coexistieron con nuevas especies que posteriormente prosperarían. Este hallazgo sugiere que las transiciones evolutivas significativas pueden ocurrir sin la destrucción masiva típica de las extinciones.

Los investigadores han propuesto el concepto de "Inflexión Biótica", que describe un punto de inflexión evolutivo donde grupos antiguos y nuevos coexisten. Factores ambientales como temperaturas cálidas, niveles del mar elevados y aguas costeras ricas en nutrientes habrían facilitado esta diversidad. Además, la conexión entre el Pacífico oriental y el Atlántico temprano a través de Colombia permitió que diferentes grupos de animales prosperaran en el mismo ecosistema.

La Formación Paja ha proporcionado un registro fósil excepcional, incluyendo reptiles marinos gigantes y una compleja red alimentaria. Este descubrimiento podría cambiar la comprensión de cómo se producen los cambios en la biodiversidad, sugiriendo que algunas transiciones evolutivas pueden estar marcadas por periodos de diversidad extraordinaria. Sin embargo, los investigadores advierten que se necesita más evidencia para determinar la frecuencia de este patrón en la historia de la Tierra.

article.explanation:
**TITULAR: APOD: 19 de noviembre de 2026 – Las nebulosas Cabeza de Caballo y de la Flama**

Las nebulosas Cabeza de Caballo y de la Flama son dos de los objetos más fascinantes del cielo nocturno, y su reciente imagen destaca su belleza y complejidad. La nebulosa Cabeza de Caballo, que se asemeja a la silueta de un caballo, se encuentra a aproximadamente 1,500 años luz de la Tierra y tiene una altura de cerca de cinco años luz. Este oscuro objeto está compuesto de polvo y gas que ocultan la luz roja de la ionización del hidrógeno, provocada por la estrella Sigma Orionis.

A la izquierda de la Cabeza de Caballo se encuentra la nebulosa de la Flama, que presenta un color anaranjado y filamentos oscuros. Esta nebulosa es un lugar activo de formación estelar, donde se están creando nuevas estrellas. Además, la imagen incluye la nebulosa de reflexión NGC 2023, que también está en proceso de formación estelar.

La captura de esta imagen requirió casi seis horas de observación en los Observatorios Remotos del Desierto de Utah, con el equipo controlado de manera remota desde Illinois, a más de 2,000 km de distancia. Este avance en la tecnología de observación astronómica permite a los científicos y aficionados explorar el cosmos de maneras innovadoras.

article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 19 – The… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Original Annotated The Horsehead and Flame Nebulas Explanation: Today’s image could have been a painting. But what do these colors mean? The brightest star, left of the center, is blue Alnitak (the Girdle): a triple star system best known for being the easternmost star in Orion’s Belt . The instantly recognizable shape of a dark horse’s head at the center is the aptly named Horsehead Nebula . It is about five light-years tall and lies approximately 1,500 light-years away. It is made of dust and gas that obscure the red glow behind it, which is caused by hydrogen gas being ionized by the bright star Sigma Orionis at the top. The orange nebula with dark filaments on the left is the Flame Nebula . Closer to the Horsehead, the blue reflection nebula NGC 2023 is actively forming stars. The data for this “painting” were collected for almost six hours at the Utah Desert Remote Observatories , but the equipment was remotely controlled by the astrophotographer from his home, over 2,000 km away in Illinois . article.explanation:
**TITULAR: APOD: 20 de noviembre de 2026 – V-G-R**  
**CATEGORÍA: espacio**

El 17 de noviembre de 2026, entusiastas de la exploración espacial se unieron para enviar un mensaje al Voyager 1, la sonda que se encuentra en el espacio interestelar. Utilizando un haz de luz, los participantes transmitieron un mensaje en código Morse que se traduce como V-G-R, el llamado de la sonda que ha estado viajando desde su lanzamiento en 1977.

Este evento fue documentado desde el Observatorio Astronómico de los Emiratos, donde se capturó la imagen del mensaje en el cielo nocturno. La distancia a la que se encuentra Voyager 1 es de aproximadamente 26 mil millones de kilómetros, lo que significa que el mensaje tardó un día en llegar a la sonda, viajando a la velocidad de la luz.

El 18 de noviembre, se confirmó que Voyager 1 alcanzó un hito significativo al llegar a una distancia de un día luz de la Tierra. Este avance resalta la longevidad y la resistencia de la misión, que ha proporcionado valiosos datos sobre nuestro sistema solar y más allá. Se estima que, a este ritmo, la sonda alcanzará un año luz en aproximadamente 18,250 años.

article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. V-G-R Explanation: On November 17, fans of interstellar spaceflight around planet Earth were invited to shine a message into the night sky. Traced by a flashlight beam switched on and off, the dashes and dots of a Morse code message captured in this time exposure from the Emirates Astronomical Observatory, are read V-G-R. That’s a call sign for the Voyager 1 spacecraft currently in interstellar space some 26 billion kilometers away. How long did it take the message to reach humanity’s most distant interstellar spacecraft ? Traveling at the speed of light, the answer is one day . In fact, the Voyager 1 spacecraft was confirmed to reach its one light-day distance milestone on November 18, at 10:16:07 UTC, nearly 50 years after launch in 1977. For extra credit, fans of math can calculate that at one light-day per 50 years, Voyager 1 will reach its one light-year (365 light-days) distance milestone in about 18,250 years.
